course.title: Astronomy: From Sky to Cosmos
course.description: Track the turning sky, weigh a planet, take a star's temperature and time the expanding universe, with real numbers throughout.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with algebra, powers of ten and ratios. Physics: Motion and Forces helps but is not required.

paragraphs: Almost everything astronomy knows has come from light, because most of what it studies is too far away to be visited or handled. A star cannot be put on a scale or touched with a thermometer, yet the colour of its light gives the temperature of its surface, the small shift in its position as Earth goes round the Sun gives its distance, and a slight stretch in the lines of its spectrum gives its speed towards or away from us. Gravity can be read in the same indirect way, since the time a moon takes to circle a planet, together with the size of its orbit, gives the planet’s mass.

What makes this possible is that a few simple laws hold everywhere. The geometry that explains why the noon Sun stands higher in summer than in winter also measures the distance to a nearby star, and the inverse-square law that weakens gravity with distance dims starlight in the same way, so that with careful reasoning and real measurements you can work out the size of a star you will only ever see as a point of light, or how long ago the expansion of the universe began.
outcomes: You’ll be able to predict how high the Sun or a star climbs from where you live, and which stars never set.
You’ll be able to explain the seasons, the phases of the Moon and why eclipses are rare.
You’ll be able to work out how long a planet takes to orbit the Sun and how fast a spacecraft must go to escape a planet.
You’ll be able to read a star’s temperature, distance and speed from its light.
You’ll be able to use the motion of distant galaxies to estimate the age of the universe.
introduction.prerequisites: You should be comfortable with algebra, ratios and powers of ten, though no astronomy is assumed.

modules.title: The sky in motion
modules.description: The turning sky, the seasons, the Moon's phases and eclipses.

modules.title: Gravity and orbits
modules.description: Kepler's laws, Newton's gravitation, orbital and escape speed, tides.

modules.title: Reading starlight
modules.description: Brightness, parallax, colour, Doppler shifts and the H–R diagram.

modules.title: Stars and the cosmos
modules.description: Stellar lifetimes and fates, Hubble's law and the Big Bang.

concepts.title: The turning sky
concepts.summary: Use latitude and declination to predict where a star climbs, and whether it ever sets.

concepts.title: Why the seasons change
concepts.summary: Explain the seasons from Earth's tilt and calculate the noon height of the Sun.

concepts.title: Phases and eclipses
concepts.summary: Relate the Moon's phase to the Sun–Earth–Moon angle and explain when eclipses happen.

concepts.title: Kepler's laws
concepts.summary: Describe an orbit by its size and shape, and link its period to its semi-major axis.

concepts.title: Newton's gravitation
concepts.summary: Use the inverse-square law of gravity to compare forces and compute surface gravity.

concepts.title: Orbits, escape and tides
concepts.summary: Compute circular and escape speeds and explain tides as a difference in pull.

concepts.title: Brightness and distance
concepts.summary: Apply the inverse-square law to starlight and measure distance by parallax.

concepts.title: Temperature, colour and motion
concepts.summary: Read a star's temperature from its colour and its motion from shifted spectral lines.

concepts.title: The H–R diagram
concepts.summary: Relate luminosity, radius and temperature, and read a star's size from its place on the diagram.

concepts.title: How mass sets a star's life
concepts.summary: Estimate main-sequence lifetimes from mass and predict how a star ends.

concepts.title: Galaxies and Hubble's law
concepts.summary: Picture the scale of the universe and use Hubble's law to link velocity and distance.

concepts.title: The age and afterglow of the Big Bang
concepts.summary: Estimate the age of the universe from H₀ and read its early heat in the microwave background.

lessons.title: The turning sky

lead.text: The turning of the sky is Earth’s own motion seen from the inside. Earth spins once on its axis and carries you round with it, while the stars are so far away that their directions in space hardly change in a night, so what changes is the way you are facing.

The figure shows Earth from above the North Pole, with a dashed line from your position to one distant star. As you are carried round, the star first lies on your horizon and then climbs above it, passes overhead and sinks back to the horizon on the far side, after which Earth itself hides it until you have been carried right round again.

afterFigure.text: Measured against the stars, one turn takes 23 hours 56 minutes, which is four minutes less than the 24 hours from one noon to the next, so a star rises about four minutes earlier each night. In whichever direction you look, **the whole sky appears to turn once a day**, and it does so because *you* turn beneath it.

diagram.alt: Earth seen from above the North Pole, with a dot for you on the rim and a dashed line to one distant star. The line keeps its direction while you are carried round, so the star sits on your horizon, climbs, passes overhead, drops to the horizon and is then hidden by Earth.
diagram.caption: Earth from above the North Pole. Use the buttons to carry you round Earth’s rim. The dashed line keeps its direction while the arrow on your dot, which points up for you, turns with Earth.

reveal.text: At 15° an hour the sky shifts by the width of the full Moon, about half a degree, in only two minutes, which is why a star seen through a fixed telescope drifts out of view so quickly.

lead.text: A wheel needs a hub, and the sky’s hub is easy to find, because the one line that stays put while Earth turns is its axis. Extend that axis far out into space in both directions and it meets the sky at two points, the **north celestial pole** above the North Pole and the **south celestial pole** above the South Pole. Every star’s circle is centred on one of these points, and the points themselves do not move.

In the northern sky a moderately bright star, Polaris, lies within a degree of the north celestial pole, so it hardly seems to move all night, and travellers have used it as a guide to north for many centuries.

afterFigure.text: The pole is easily confused with the point straight above your head, which is called the **zenith**. The two coincide only at the North Pole itself. Everywhere else the zenith is fixed by where you stand and sweeps across the stars as Earth turns, whereas the celestial pole is fixed by Earth’s axis alone and stays *among* the stars.

diagram.alt: Earth in cross-section with its axis drawn from the South Pole to the North Pole and extended out to the north and south celestial poles. A second view adds an observer whose zenith is a different spot from the celestial pole.
diagram.caption: Earth in cross-section, with its axis extended out to the sky. The point overhead is a different spot from the pole.

lead.text: How the hub sits in your sky depends on where you stand, as an imagined walk from the equator to the North Pole shows. On the equator Earth’s axis lies along your horizon, so the north celestial pole sits on the northern horizon, and even a star close to it spends *half* of each turn below the horizon.

As you walk north **the pole lifts away from the horizon**, and when you reach the North Pole the axis points straight up, so the pole stands at your zenith and every star circles it at a constant height without rising or setting.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows three stops on the walk. Between the first and the last the pole climbs steadily from the horizon to the zenith, which suggests a rule linking its height to how far north you have travelled, and the next screen gives names to the two quantities that the rule connects.

diagram.alt: A sketch of the northern sky for three places: the equator, a place partway to the pole, and the North Pole. The north celestial pole sits on the horizon at the equator, partway up the sky at the middle place and straight overhead at the North Pole.
diagram.caption: The northern sky seen from three places. On the equator the pole sits on the horizon and stars rise and set. At the North Pole it stands overhead and every star circles without setting.

lead.text: To say how far north you are, geographers use **latitude**, the angle at the centre of Earth between the equator and the line from the centre to you. It is 0° on the equator, 90° at the North Pole and about 52° in Amsterdam, and since Earth’s radius is 6,371 km each degree corresponds to about 111 km along the ground, which puts Amsterdam some 5,800 km north of the equator.

To say how high something is in the sky, astronomers use **altitude**, the angle measured at your feet from the horizon up to the object. A star on the horizon has an altitude of 0°, the zenith has an altitude of 90°, and a star halfway up the sky stands at 45°.

afterFigure.text: Because the two angles are measured in different places, one at the centre of Earth and the other at your feet, they might seem to have nothing to do with each other. The walk has already suggested otherwise, since the [[north celestial pole|The point in the sky where Earth’s axis points. Met earlier in this lesson.]] has an altitude and the walker has a latitude, and both rise from 0° to 90° over the same journey.

diagram.alt: Three views for the two measures. One shows Earth in cross-section with the angle of latitude at the centre for an observer at Amsterdam. One places observers at 0, 52 and 90 degrees. One shows a star at an altitude of 35 degrees above the horizon, with the zenith at 90 degrees.
diagram.caption: Latitude is an angle taken at Earth’s centre. Altitude is an angle taken at your feet, from the horizon up to the object. Use the buttons to move between the two.

reveal.text: That prediction rests on a pattern in two points, which is not yet a reason, and the next screen supplies the reason.

lead.text: The pattern holds at every latitude, and a short piece of geometry shows why. Call your latitude φ, the angle at Earth’s centre between the equator and the line to you. Your horizon is at right angles to that line, because “up” for you points directly away from the centre.

Now draw an arrow from your position towards the [[celestial pole|The point where Earth’s axis meets the sky. Met earlier in this lesson.]]. The pole is so distant that it lies in the same direction from every place on Earth, so this **pole arrow** runs parallel to the axis. The axis is at right angles to the equator, so it makes an angle of 90° − φ with the line to you, and the pole arrow, being parallel to it, leans away from straight up by the same 90° − φ.

afterFigure.text: Your horizon is 90° from straight up, so the pole arrow stands 90° − (90° − φ) = φ above the horizon, which is its [[altitude|The angle measured up from the horizon to an object. Met earlier in this lesson.]]. *Whatever* your latitude, **the altitude of the north celestial pole equals your latitude**, which is 0° on the equator, 52° in Amsterdam and 90° at the North Pole, as the walk suggested.

diagram.alt: Earth in cross-section built up in four steps for an observer at latitude 52 degrees: the angle of latitude, then the horizon at a right angle to the line to the centre, then the pole arrow parallel to the axis, then the angle between the horizon and the pole arrow, which equals the latitude.

reveal.text: Polaris lies a little under a degree from the true pole, so the result is good to about a degree, and navigators removed most of that offset with a small correction from published tables.

lead.text: The same projection that gave the poles gives a second reference line. Extend Earth’s equator out into the sky and it becomes the **celestial equator**, a circle halfway between the two celestial poles. A star’s position north or south of it is its **declination**, measured in degrees in the same way as [[latitude|The angle at Earth’s centre between the equator and the line to you. Met earlier in this lesson.]], starting from 0° on the celestial equator, with a plus sign for stars north of it and a minus sign for stars south of it.

A star’s declination does not change during the night, because the sky turns as one wheel, so each star keeps a fixed distance from the poles. A star at declination δ lies 90° − δ from the north celestial pole and circles it at that distance: a star at +30° goes round on a circle of radius 60°, a star on the celestial equator on a circle of radius 90°, and a star at −30° on a circle of radius 120°.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows these three stars as seen from 52° N. The celestial equator is the dividing case, since a star on it spends exactly half of its circle above the horizon, so the star at +30° is up for *more* than half of each turn and the star at −30° for less.

lead.text: Whether a star ever sets depends on whether the whole of its circle lies above the horizon. The pole stands φ above the horizon, and a star at [[declination|A star’s angle north or south of the celestial equator. Met earlier in this lesson.]] δ circles it at a distance of 90° − δ, so at the lowest point of its circle, directly below the pole, the star’s altitude is φ − (90° − δ). It never sets if that stays above 0°, which gives the condition **δ > 90° − φ**, and a star that satisfies it is called **circumpolar**, meaning that it circles the pole without touching the horizon.

At Amsterdam, where φ = 52°, the limit is 90° − 52° = 38°, so every star north of +38° is up all night. A star at +70° clears the horizon at its lowest point by 32°, while a star at +30° dips 8° below it. Move the +70° star to a place at 10° N, where the limit is 80°, and it too begins to rise and set.

afterFigure.text: The limit grows as you go south and reaches 90° on the equator, which no star exceeds, so no star there is circumpolar. By the same reasoning a star more than 90° − φ *south* of the celestial equator never rises at all for an observer in the north.

reveal.text: The star at +60° has a lowest point 10° above the horizon, while the star at +45° has a lowest point 5° below it, so the boundary lies between them.

lessons.orientation: How the turning sky depends on where you stand: the height of the celestial pole, declination, and which stars never set.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Leave a camera pointing at the northern sky with the shutter open for a few hours, and every star comes out as a short arc of a circle, all of the arcs curving about **one point**. Stars close to that point draw small circles and stars far from it draw large ones, but none of them behaves differently from the rest, as though the whole sky were *a single wheel* turning about a fixed hub.

The wheel goes once round in about a day, and where its hub sits depends on where you stand: from Amsterdam it is a little over halfway from the horizon to the point overhead, and from the North Pole it is directly above you. Working out how the hub’s height follows from your position on Earth gives two practical results, a way to find how far north you are from a single star and a way to say in advance which stars never set.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to work out how high the sky’s hub stands from your latitude, and which stars never set.

recap.keyIdea: The sky turns once a day about the celestial poles, the pole’s altitude equals your latitude, and a star never sets when its declination is greater than 90° minus your latitude.

blocks.text: The sky appears to turn through 15° an hour because Earth turns beneath it, and the hub of that turning is the [[celestial pole|The point where Earth’s axis meets the sky. Met in “The turning sky”.]], which stands as high above your horizon as your latitude, from 0° on the equator to 90° at the North Pole.

A star’s declination fixes the size of its circle about the pole, so from latitude φ every star with a declination above 90° − φ is **circumpolar**, while the stars that lie far enough south of the celestial equator never rise.

recap.nextHook: The Sun belongs to the same turning sky, but its declination changes through the year, and a stick pushed into the ground shows the effect, because the length of its noon shadow grows and shrinks from season to season.

lessons.title: Why the seasons change

lead.text: Earth’s axis is not upright with respect to its orbit. It leans by 23.4° from the perpendicular to the plane in which Earth goes round the Sun, a lean called the **axial tilt**, and as Earth travels round the Sun in a year the axis keeps pointing at the *same* place in the sky, which is why Polaris stays at the pole whatever the date.

The consequence is that the hemisphere leaning towards the Sun changes as Earth moves round. About 21 June the north leans towards the Sun as far as it ever does, and about 21 December it leans as far away as it ever does, and these two dates are the **solstices**. Midway between them, about 20 March and 22 September, the axis leans neither towards the Sun nor away from it, and these dates are the **equinoxes**.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows Earth at three of these dates, with an observer at 45° N marked. The observer stays at the same latitude throughout, but the angle at which the Sun’s rays arrive changes with the date, and the next screen puts a number on that change.

lead.text: In the first lesson a star’s [[declination|A star’s angle north or south of the celestial equator. Met in “The turning sky”.]] stayed fixed, but the Sun’s does not, because Earth’s position changes as the year goes on. At the June solstice the north leans towards the Sun, so the Sun lies 23.4° north of the celestial equator, with a declination of +23.4°. At the equinoxes it lies on the celestial equator, with a declination of 0°, and at the December solstice it lies 23.4° south, with a declination of −23.4°.

The Sun is directly overhead at any place whose latitude equals its declination, since the zenith of a place at latitude φ lies at declination φ in the sky. At the June solstice that place is on the line of latitude 23.4° N, the **Tropic of Cancer**, and at the December solstice it is on the line 23.4° S, the **Tropic of Capricorn**, while at the equinoxes the overhead Sun is on the equator.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the three cases. Between the tropics the overhead point crosses the equator twice a year, and **no place outside the tropics ever has the Sun directly overhead**, because the Sun never goes beyond 23.4° of declination.

lead.text: At noon the Sun stands on the line running from the north point of the horizon through the zenith to the south point, and it is at its highest for the day. The [[zenith|The point in the sky straight above you. Met in “The turning sky”.]] of a place at latitude φ lies at declination φ, so the Sun at declination δ is a gap of |φ − δ| from the zenith, and its **noon altitude**, the Sun’s height at its highest, is **90° − |φ − δ|**. The bars mean that the gap counts as a positive number whichever of φ and δ is larger.

For an observer at 35° N at the June solstice, δ = +23.4°, so the gap is 35° − 23.4° = 11.6° and the Sun reaches 90° − 11.6° = 78.4°. At 60° N the gap is 36.6° and the Sun reaches only 53.4°. At 15° N the Sun passes 8.4° north of the zenith, since δ is now larger than φ, and the same rule gives 90° − 8.4° = 81.6°.

afterFigure.text: The rule needs nothing but subtraction, so it works on any date once the Sun’s declination is known, and the next two questions use it for London at the two solstices.

reveal.text: A stick 1 m tall would cast a noon shadow of 1 m ÷ tan 61.9°, about 0.53 m, which is the short June shadow described at the start.

lead.text: In winter the Sun’s declination is negative, and **the rule needs no change**, because a negative number is subtracted in the same way as any other. At 40° N in December, δ = −23.4°, so the gap |40° − (−23.4°)| is 63.4° and the noon altitude is 90° − 63.4° = 26.6°.

South of the equator the latitude is negative too, so the [[noon altitude|The Sun’s height above the horizon at noon. Met earlier in this lesson.]] rule is used with a minus sign on φ. At 20° S, φ = −20°, and in June the Sun’s declination is +23.4°, so the gap is |−20° − 23.4°| = 43.4° and the noon Sun stands at 46.6°. In December, δ = −23.4°, so the gap is only |−20° + 23.4°| = 3.4° and the noon Sun stands at 86.6°, almost overhead.

afterFigure.text: Because the tilt gives one hemisphere a high Sun at the moment it gives the other a low one, the two hemispheres have *opposite* seasons on any given date, and that fact returns later in the lesson as evidence about the cause.

reveal.text: The same stick would cast a shadow of 1 ÷ tan 15.1° = 3.7 times its height, which accounts for the long December shadow in the opening.

lead.text: A high noon Sun and a low one differ in more than the length of a shadow. Sunlight arrives in parallel rays, and a beam of a given width falling on level ground when the Sun is at altitude h lands on a patch 1/sin h times as wide, so **the lower the Sun, the thinner its light** is spread over the ground, as the [[altitude|The angle measured up from the horizon to an object. Met in “The turning sky”.]] of the Sun falls.

In the figure the same beam falls once with the Sun at 60° and once with it at 30°. The patch covers 1.15 times the beam’s width in the first case and twice its width in the second, so each square metre of ground in the second case receives about half as much light.

afterFigure.text: London’s noon Sun at the December solstice, at 15.1°, spreads its beam over 1/sin 15.1° = 3.8 times its width, against 1/sin 61.9° = 1.1 times in June, so each square metre of ground receives *less than a third* as much light at noon in December. The December day is also under 8 hours long, against about 16½ hours in June, and the two effects together make midwinter in London cold and midsummer warm.

diagram.alt: The same beam of sunlight falling on level ground twice. With the Sun 60 degrees above the horizon the patch of ground it covers is 1.15 times as wide as the beam, and with the Sun 30 degrees above the horizon it covers a patch twice as wide.
diagram.caption: One beam of sunlight, drawn twice. The lower the Sun, the longer the patch of ground the same beam has to cover. Use the buttons to compare the two.

lead.text: It is natural to suppose that Earth is nearer the Sun in summer, but the orbit does not support that. Earth’s distance from the Sun varies from about 147.1 million km in early January to about 152.1 million km in early July, a change of only about 3%, and the planet is nearest the Sun in *the middle of the northern winter*.

A second observation settles the matter. If distance caused the seasons, both hemispheres would be warm at the same time, whereas the southern hemisphere has summer while the north has winter. **The tilt explains the reversal at once**, because the same lean that raises the Sun for one hemisphere lowers it for the other.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows an observer at 25° N, where the noon Sun stands 88.4° high at the June solstice and 41.6° high in December, a swing of nearly 47° that **the tilt alone produces**.

reveal.text: On the equator at an equinox the gap is 0°, so the noon Sun passes through the zenith, which is why the equator has the Sun overhead twice a year.
Without tilt every noon would look like an equinox in London, with the Sun at the same height and 12 hours of daylight on every date, and there would be no seasons from the Sun’s height at all.

lessons.orientation: Why the Sun’s noon height changes through the year: the tilt of Earth’s axis, the Sun’s declination and the rule for noon altitude.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Push a straight stick upright into level ground in London and measure its shadow at noon on the longest day of the year in June, and the shadow comes out at **roughly half the length of the stick**. Measure it again at noon in December and it is *nearly four times* as long as the stick, so the winter shadow is about seven times the length of the summer one.

Nothing about the stick has changed, and the Sun is no nearer or farther in any way that matters, so the difference has to lie in *the direction from which its light arrives*. Following the Sun’s path through the year with the angles of the first lesson shows that the Sun’s declination, unlike a star’s, is not fixed but swings between two limits, and that this swing is what produces the seasons.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to explain the seasons from Earth’s tilt and work out the Sun’s noon height for any latitude and date.

recap.keyIdea: Earth’s axis is tilted by 23.4° and keeps pointing the same way, so the Sun’s declination swings between +23.4° and −23.4°, and the noon altitude is 90° minus the gap between your latitude and that declination.

blocks.text: Because the axis keeps its direction while Earth orbits, the hemisphere leaning towards the Sun changes with the date, and the Sun’s [[declination|A star’s angle north or south of the celestial equator. Met in “The turning sky”.]] runs from +23.4° at the June solstice through 0° at the equinoxes to −23.4° in December.

At noon the Sun stands 90° − |φ − δ| above the horizon, and a low Sun both spreads its light over more ground and shines for fewer hours, which makes the tilt, and not the 3% change in Earth’s distance, the cause of the seasons.

recap.nextHook: The Sun is not the only body whose changing position fills the sky, because the Moon, which shines by the Sun’s light, runs through its phases in about a month, and the next lesson shows how the angle between the Sun, Earth and Moon produces them.

lessons.title: Phases and eclipses

lead.text: The Moon gives no light of its own. The Sun lights whichever half of it faces the Sun, and that half is lit all the time, whatever we see from Earth. What changes from night to night is how much of the lit half is turned towards us, and that depends on the **Sun–Earth–Moon angle**, the angle at Earth between the direction of the Sun and the direction of the Moon.

At new moon the Moon lies almost in the direction of the Sun, so the angle is about 0° and the lit half faces away from us, and we see only the dark side. At full moon the Moon lies opposite the Sun, the angle is 180°, and the whole of the lit half faces us. In between we see part of the lit half, and the shape of the part we see is called the Moon’s **phase**.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows three positions. As the Moon travels round Earth the angle grows steadily, from 0° at new moon through 180° at full moon and on to 360° at the next new moon, which takes about a month, and *the phase follows the angle exactly*.

lead.text: A phase can be given a number. The share of the visible disc that is lit is **(1 − cos θ) ÷ 2**, where θ is the [[Sun–Earth–Moon angle|The angle at Earth between the direction of the Sun and the direction of the Moon. Met earlier in this lesson.]]. At new moon θ = 0° and cos θ = 1, so the share is 0, and at full moon θ = 180° and cos θ = −1, so the share is 1, the whole disc. For angles in between the cosine takes values between 1 and −1, which gives every share from 0 to 1.

The shapes have names. When less than half of the disc is lit the Moon is a **crescent**, and when more than half is lit it is **gibbous**. When exactly half is lit we speak of a **quarter moon**, because the Moon is then a quarter of the way round its cycle. Between new moon and full moon the lit part grows and the Moon is *waxing*, and after full moon the lit part shrinks and the Moon is *waning*.

afterFigure.text: At 150° the share is (1 − cos 150°) ÷ 2 = (1 + 0.866) ÷ 2 = 0.933, so the Moon is a waxing gibbous with 93% of its disc lit, and at 30° the same calculation gives (1 − 0.866) ÷ 2 = 0.067, a thin crescent. The two shares add up to 1, because cos (180° − θ) is always the negative of cos θ.

lead.text: The Moon takes 27.32 days to return to the same place among the stars, but its phases take longer to repeat, because a phase depends on where the Moon is relative to the Sun, and the Sun does not stay put. While the Moon goes once round, Earth moves along its orbit and the Sun appears to shift by about 27° against the stars, so the Moon has to travel that far again to catch up.

That extra 27° takes just over two days, which makes a cycle of 29.53 days from one new moon to the next. This interval is the **synodic month**, and it is the time taken by one full turn of the [[Sun–Earth–Moon angle|The angle at Earth between the direction of the Sun and the direction of the Moon. Met earlier in this lesson.]], and so the number that fixes the calendar of the Moon’s phases.

afterFigure.text: One synodic month therefore carries the angle through a full 360°, and since the Moon travels steadily, the angle grows at a steady rate each day, which the next question asks you to find.

reveal.text: With the sky turning at 15° an hour, a gain of 12.2° a day means the Moon rises about 12.2° ÷ 15° per hour = 0.81 hours, or roughly 49 minutes, later each night.

lead.text: Full moon and new moon are the two moments when the Sun, Earth and Moon come closest to a straight line, and that is the arrangement an eclipse needs. At full moon, with Earth between the Sun and the Moon, the Moon can pass through Earth’s shadow, which darkens it in a **lunar eclipse**. At new moon, with the Moon between the Sun and Earth, the Moon’s shadow can fall on Earth, and anyone standing in it sees the Sun covered in a **solar eclipse**.

Suppose the Moon’s orbit lay in the same plane as Earth’s, so that the Moon’s path across the sky ran along the **ecliptic**, the path the Sun itself follows through the stars in the course of a year, which the last lesson used. Then every full moon would be eclipsed and every new moon would cover the Sun, giving about two dozen eclipses a year. There are far fewer, which means that something about the Moon’s orbit must differ, and the next screen finds out what.

The Moon’s orbit is tilted by about 5.1° to the [[ecliptic|The path the Sun follows against the stars through the year, in the plane of Earth’s orbit. Met earlier in this lesson.]], so the Moon spends half of each circuit north of it and half south, crossing it at two points. At a distance of 384,400 km a tilt of 5.1° can lift the Moon 384,400 × sin 5.1°, about 34,000 km, above or below the plane, which is far more than the 9,000 km or so across Earth’s shadow at that distance, so at most full moons the shadow passes above or below the Moon, and at most new moons the Moon’s shadow passes above or below Earth.

An eclipse is therefore possible only when a full or new moon falls *near* one of the two crossing points, so that the Moon lies within about a degree of the ecliptic. That happens in two short periods each year, about six months apart, and even then the alignment has to be close.

afterFigure.text: In the figure a full moon only 0.4° from the ecliptic passes through the shadow, while a full moon 4.5° north of it and a new moon 3° south of it both miss, which is how **most months pass without an eclipse**.

cases.label: Full moon 4.5° north of the ecliptic
New moon 3° south of the ecliptic

lead.text: Whether the Moon can hide the Sun depends on how large each looks in the sky, and that is measured by an angle. The **angular diameter** of an object is the angle between the directions to its two edges. For a small angle it equals the object’s diameter divided by its distance, which gives the angle in *radians*, the unit in which an angle is the length of the arc divided by the radius, and one radian is 57.3°, so multiplying by 57.3 converts the result to degrees.

The Sun is 1.39 million km across and 149.6 million km away, so its angular diameter is 1.39 ÷ 149.6 = 0.00929 radians, and 0.00929 × 57.3 = 0.532°. The same method works for any object whose size and distance are known, and it gives the quantity that decides whether the Moon can cover the Sun, which the next question settles.

reveal.text: The Moon’s 0.52° is almost the Sun’s 0.53°, because the Sun is about 400 times as wide as the Moon and about 400 times as far away, so the Moon can just cover the Sun, and covers it completely only when it happens to be nearer than average.

lessons.orientation: How the Sun–Earth–Moon angle sets the Moon’s phase, how long the cycle lasts, and why eclipses are rarer than full and new moons.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: At first quarter the Moon is a half disc, and a few days earlier it was a thin sliver whose lit edge faced the Sun and never turned away from it. Nothing about the Moon itself changes from night to night: it is always a ball with *one half lit by the Sun*, so the changing shapes must come from the angle at which we look at that lit half.

The same angle decides when the Moon can darken the Sun, or be darkened itself, in an eclipse, and it explains something that seems strange at first, which is that eclipses do not occur every month, although the Moon passes close to the line between the Sun and Earth once at new moon and once at full moon. Working through that geometry gives the lit share of the Moon on any night from a single angle, and it shows that at most new and full moons the Moon passes a little above or below that line, so that **the shadows usually miss**.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to find how much of the Moon is lit on any night, and why eclipses are rare.

recap.keyIdea: The Moon is always half lit, its phase is set by the Sun–Earth–Moon angle, which turns through 360° every 29.53 days, and eclipses are rare because the Moon’s orbit is tilted to the ecliptic.

blocks.text: The share of the Moon’s disc that is lit is (1 − cos θ) ÷ 2, where θ is the [[Sun–Earth–Moon angle|The angle at Earth between the direction of the Sun and the direction of the Moon. Met in “Phases and eclipses”.]], and θ turns through a full 360° in the 29.53 days of a synodic month, a little longer than the 27.32 days that the Moon takes to return to the same stars.

A lunar eclipse needs a full moon and a solar eclipse needs a new moon, but the Moon’s orbit is **tilted by 5.1°** to the ecliptic, so only the full and new moons that fall near the two crossing points line up, and the Moon can cover the Sun because it looks almost exactly as wide.

recap.nextHook: The Moon’s path round Earth is one example of an orbit, and the next lesson describes any orbit by its size and its shape, and shows how the time taken for a circuit follows from its size.

lessons.title: Kepler’s laws

lead.text: An **ellipse** is easy to draw. Push two pins into a board, loop a piece of string loosely round them, and pull the loop taut with a pencil, and as the pencil moves round, always keeping the string tight, it draws an ellipse. Each pin marks a **focus** of the ellipse, and the two together are its foci. The shape depends only on how far apart the pins are, and with both pins at the same spot the string draws a circle, so a circle is the special case in which the two foci coincide.

Kepler’s **first law**, published in 1609 in his *Astronomia Nova*, says that each planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at *one* focus. The other focus is empty, and the Sun does not sit at the middle of the orbit, which is why a planet’s distance from the Sun changes as it goes round.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the pins are first close together and then far apart, so the ellipse becomes longer and thinner, and the Sun sits at one of the two foci in each.

lead.text: The longest line across an ellipse passes through both foci, and half of its length is the **semi-major axis**, written a, which is the number that gives the size of an orbit. The point of the orbit nearest the Sun is **perihelion** and the point farthest from it is **aphelion**, and since *both* lie on that long line with the Sun between them, their two distances add up to the whole line, so perihelion + aphelion = 2a.

Distances in the solar system are measured in the **astronomical unit**, or AU, which is about 149.6 million km and is the average distance from Earth to the Sun. Earth’s distance runs from 147.1 million km at perihelion in early January to 152.1 million km at aphelion in early July, which add up to 299.2 million km, so its semi-major axis is half of that, 149.6 million km, or 1 AU.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the same shape at two sizes, with a = 3 AU and a = 1.5 AU. Halving a halves every distance in the orbit, perihelion and aphelion included, and the next screen deals with the shape separately.

lead.text: Two orbits can have the same semi-major axis and quite different shapes, and the shape is measured by the **eccentricity**, written e. It is the distance from the centre of the ellipse to a focus, divided by a, so it is 0 for a circle, where the focus is at the centre, and it approaches 1 as the ellipse becomes long and thin.

The Sun sits a distance a × e from the centre, which fixes the two extreme distances. The near end of the orbit lies a from the centre and the Sun lies a × e from the centre *towards* it, so **perihelion is a(1 − e)**, and in the same way aphelion is a(1 + e). For a = 3 AU and e = 0.5 the perihelion is 3 × 0.5 = 1.5 AU and the aphelion is 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 AU, which add up to 6 AU, or 2a, as they must.

afterFigure.text: Planetary orbits are mostly close to circles, with e = 0.017 for Earth and e = 0.093 for Mars. Comets can be very different, and Halley’s comet, with e = 0.967 and a = 17.8 AU, comes within 0.59 AU of the Sun and recedes to about 35 AU.

reveal.text: Mars, with a = 1.52 AU and e = 0.093, has a perihelion of 1.52 × 0.907 = 1.38 AU and an aphelion of 1.52 × 1.093 = 1.66 AU, which is why its orbit looks almost circular.

lead.text: Kepler’s **second law** concerns the speed along the orbit. Draw a line from the Sun to the planet, and as the planet moves the line sweeps out area; the law says that it sweeps out *equal areas in equal times*. Near [[perihelion|The point of an orbit nearest the Sun. Met earlier in this lesson.]] the line is short, so the planet has to cover more of its orbit in a given time to sweep out the same area as the much longer line sweeps near aphelion, which means that the planet moves fastest at perihelion and slowest at [[aphelion|The point of an orbit farthest from the Sun. Met earlier in this lesson.]].

At the two ends of the long axis the planet moves at right angles to the line from the Sun, and the area swept in a short time is half the line’s length times the distance travelled, so equal areas mean that speed × distance from the Sun is the same at both ends. The ratio of the two speeds is therefore the *inverse* of the ratio of the distances, so that **speed at perihelion ÷ speed at aphelion = aphelion distance ÷ perihelion distance**.

afterFigure.text: Earth shows the effect in a small way. It moves at 30.3 km/s at perihelion in January and at 29.3 km/s at aphelion in July, a ratio of 1.03, which equals the ratio of the distances, 152.1 ÷ 147.1.

reveal.text: A planet four times as fast at perihelion covers four times as much of its path in the same time, yet it sweeps the same area, because its line to the Sun is a quarter as long.

lead.text: Kepler’s **third law**, published in 1619 in his *Harmonices Mundi*, connects the size of an orbit with the time taken to go once round it. That time is the **period**, P, and when P is measured in years and a in AU the law takes the form **P² = a³**, the same for every planet in the solar system.

For Earth the [[semi-major axis|Half the longest line across an ellipse, the number that gives the size of an orbit. Met earlier in this lesson.]] is a = 1 AU, so a³ = 1 and P = 1 year, which is how the units were chosen. Mars has a = 1.52 AU, so a³ = 1.52³ = 3.51 and P = √3.51 = 1.87 years, in agreement with the 1.88 years that Mars actually takes. A planet farther out therefore takes longer to go round, and by more than its distance alone would suggest, because its path is longer and it also moves more slowly.

The form P² = a³ holds for the Sun. For a star of mass M, measured in **solar masses** (one solar mass is the mass of the Sun, 1.989 × 10³⁰ kg), the law becomes **P² = a³ ÷ M**, so a heavier star gives a *shorter* [[period|The time an orbit takes to go once round. Met earlier in this lesson.]] at the same distance. The planet’s own mass is so small beside the star’s that it can be ignored.

A planet at 1 AU from a star of 9 solar masses has P² = 1³ ÷ 9 = 1/9, so P = 1/3 year, or 4 months, a third of Earth’s year. The star’s stronger gravity pulls the planet round faster, and the next lesson explains why that follows from Newton’s law of gravitation.

reveal.text: Four solar masses halves the period, because the square root of 4 is 2, and in general doubling a star’s mass shortens a planet’s year by a factor of √2, about 1.41.

lessons.orientation: How an orbit is described by its size and shape, how speed changes along it, and how the period follows from the size.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: For nearly two thousand years astronomers took it for granted that the planets move in circles, since a circle is the simplest closed curve and the heavens were thought to deserve the simplest motion. Johannes Kepler, working in the early 1600s from the naked-eye observations of Tycho Brahe, tried a circle for Mars and found that the best circle still missed Tycho’s positions by **8 arcminutes**, about a quarter of the width of the full Moon.

Most people would have put so small a gap down to error. Kepler trusted Tycho’s accuracy, which was good to an [[arcminute|One sixtieth of a degree. The full Moon is about 31 arcminutes across. Met in “Phases and eclipses” as 0.52°.]] or two, and concluded that the circle itself was wrong. That decision led him to three laws that describe every orbit in the solar system and, as later lessons show, every orbit of one body about another: the *shape* of an orbit, the speed along it, and the time it takes.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to find an orbit’s nearest and farthest distances, and its period from its size.

recap.keyIdea: An orbit is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus, a planet moves fastest at perihelion, and the square of the period equals the cube of the semi-major axis divided by the star’s mass in solar masses.

blocks.text: The size of an orbit is its [[semi-major axis|Half the longest line across an ellipse, written a. Met in “Kepler’s laws”.]] a, its shape is its eccentricity e, and the nearest and farthest distances are a(1 − e) and a(1 + e), which add up to 2a.

Because the line from the Sun to the planet sweeps equal areas in equal times, **the speeds at the two ends are in the inverse ratio of the distances**, and the period follows P² = a³ ÷ M, with P in years, a in AU and M in solar masses.

recap.nextHook: Kepler found these laws by fitting them to Tycho’s data, without saying why they hold, and Newton later showed that all three follow from a single law of gravitation, which the next lesson introduces.

lessons.title: Newton’s gravitation

lead.text: Newton asked whether the force that pulls an apple to the ground also holds the Moon in its orbit. A body left alone moves in a straight line, so the Moon must be pulled continually away from that line towards Earth, and the size of the pull shows in how far the Moon drops below its straight path. In one second the Moon travels 1,023 m along its orbit and drops 1.4 mm out of line, while an apple falls 4.9 m from rest, so the pull at the Moon is far weaker than the pull at the apple.

The ratio of the two falls is about 3,600, and 3,600 is 60 × 60. The Moon is about 60 times as far from the centre of Earth as the apple is, since Earth’s radius is 6,371 km and the Moon’s distance is 384,400 km, so the pull has weakened by the *square* of the distance ratio. A force that varies in this way follows an **inverse-square law**, under which doubling the distance divides the force by 2², or 4.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the same pair of bodies at separations of 1 and 2 units, and the force at the larger separation is a quarter of the force at the smaller, as the law requires.

lead.text: Distance is only part of the law. The pull between two bodies is proportional to the mass of each, so doubling one mass doubles the force and doubling both quadruples it, and the [[inverse-square law|A force that falls to a quarter when the distance doubles. Met earlier in this lesson.]] supplies the dependence on distance. Putting the two dependences together gives Newton’s **law of gravitation**, F = GMm ÷ r², where M and m are the masses, r is the distance between their centres, and G is the **gravitational constant**, 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², which fixes the strength of gravity.

G is so small that two 1 kg masses 1 m apart attract each other with a force of only 6.7 × 10⁻¹¹ N, which is why gravity is noticeable only when at least one of the bodies is as large as a planet. The force acts on both bodies equally. The Sun pulls on Earth with exactly the force with which Earth pulls on the Sun, although the Sun is about 333,000 times as massive, because the same force changes the speed of a small mass a great deal and the speed of a large mass only a little.

afterFigure.text: To compare two situations, multiply the factors by which each quantity changes. Doubling one mass and doubling the distance gives a factor of 2 for the mass and 1/2² = 1/4 for the distance, so the force becomes 2 × 1/4 = 1/2 of what it was. The figure shows masses of 1 and 1, and then 4 and 1, at the same separation, where **the force is four times as large**.

lead.text: A force F on a mass m gives it an **acceleration** of F ÷ m, the rate at which its speed changes, as Newton’s second law states. When the force is gravity, F = GMm ÷ r², so the acceleration is GM ÷ r², and **the falling mass cancels**. How fast an object accelerates under gravity therefore depends on *the body that pulls it*, through M, and on the distance r, but not on the object’s own mass.

The quantity GM ÷ r² is the **gravitational field** at distance r from a body of mass M, and it is measured in m/s², the acceleration that any object placed there would have. In 1971 the Apollo 15 commander David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather together on the Moon, where no air held the feather back, and they reached the ground at the same moment, because both fell in the same field.

On the surface of a world of mass M and radius R the distance to its centre is R, so the field there is **g = GM ÷ R²**, the [[gravitational field|The acceleration GM ÷ r² that any object has at distance r from a body of mass M. Met earlier in this lesson.]] at the surface. Tables give the product GM directly, because the orbits of satellites measure it far more precisely than G and M can be found separately, and they give R in kilometres, which must be converted to metres before the formula is used.

For the Moon, GM = 4.9 × 10¹² m³/s² and R = 1,737 km = 1.737 × 10⁶ m, so R² = 3.017 × 10¹² m² and g = 4.9 × 10¹² ÷ 3.017 × 10¹² = 1.62 m/s². That is about a sixth of Earth’s surface value, which is why the Apollo astronauts could bound across the lunar surface.

afterFigure.text: The field weakens with height, but slowly, because the distance from the centre grows by only a small fraction of Earth’s radius: at 400 km up, where the International Space Station orbits, g is still 89% of its surface value, so astronauts there are not beyond Earth’s gravity but *falling freely* in it, a point the next lesson takes up.

reveal.text: Saturn, with about 95 times Earth’s mass and 9.4 times its radius, has a surface field of 95 ÷ 9.4² ≈ 1.1 times Earth’s, which shows how a large radius dilutes the pull of a large mass.

lessons.orientation: How the pull of gravity changes with distance and mass, and how to find the field at the surface of a world.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Kepler’s laws say how a planet moves, and they leave open why it should move that way. Isaac Newton’s answer, set out in his *Principia* of 1687, began with a comparison between two falling things. An apple dropped from a branch falls about 4.9 m in its first second, while the Moon, in each second of its orbit, falls only about 1.4 mm below the straight line that it would follow if nothing pulled it.

The two falls differ by a *definite factor*, and from that factor Newton drew **a rule for how the pull of gravity changes with distance**. Extended to every pair of masses, the rule becomes a law of gravitation, and with it you can work out the pull at the surface of any world from its mass and radius, from the Moon to Mars.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to compare gravitational forces for any change of distance or mass, and find a world’s surface gravity.

recap.keyIdea: Gravity weakens as the inverse square of the distance and grows with the product of the masses, and dividing out the falling mass gives the field g = GM ÷ r², the same for every object.

blocks.text: The force between two masses is F = GMm ÷ r², so changes to the masses multiply and a change in the distance acts through its *square*, and the pull on each body is the same as the pull on the other.

Dividing the force by the mass that is pulled leaves the [[gravitational field|The acceleration GM ÷ r² that any object has at distance r from a body of mass M. Met in “Newton’s gravitation”.]], so that at the surface of a world g = GM ÷ R² depends on the world’s mass and radius and not on the falling object.

recap.nextHook: Gravity is also what keeps a satellite in its orbit, and the next lesson uses the field to find how fast an object must move to stay in orbit round a planet, and how fast it must move to escape.

lessons.title: Orbits, escape and tides

lead.text: Newton pictured a cannon on a very high mountain, firing a ball horizontally. Gravity pulls the ball down from the first instant, so it follows a curve and lands, and the harder the cannon fires, the farther away it lands. Because Earth is round, the ground curves away beneath the ball as it travels, so that for a fast enough shot the ground falls away as quickly as the ball falls towards it.

At that speed the ball falls continually without ever reaching the ground, and it circles Earth and comes back to the cannon, which is what **being in orbit** means: an orbit is *free fall* with enough sideways speed to keep missing. A slower ball lands, and a faster one swings out to a higher and longer orbit, until at a still greater speed it does not return at all.

afterFigure.text: Every orbit therefore has a speed that goes with it, fixed by the pull of the planet and the distance from its centre, and the next question gives the numbers for the lowest orbit of all, just above Earth’s surface.

reveal.text: That is the circular orbital speed at Earth’s surface, more exactly 7.9 km/s, and a ball launched at it would circle Earth just above the ground if there were no air and no mountains.

lead.text: The same condition gives a formula. A body moving at speed v on a circle of radius r is accelerating towards the centre at v² ÷ r, and in a circular orbit the only thing supplying that acceleration is gravity, whose field at distance r is GM ÷ r². Setting the two equal gives v² ÷ r = GM ÷ r², so that **v = √(GM ÷ r)**, the **circular speed** at distance r from the centre of a body of mass M.

Two features matter. The speed does not depend on the mass of the satellite, since the [[gravitational field|The acceleration GM ÷ r² that any object has at distance r from a body of mass M. Met in “Newton’s gravitation”.]] does not, and it falls as r grows, so higher orbits are *slower*. For the Moon, at r = 384,400 km = 3.844 × 10⁸ m, v = √(3.986 × 10¹⁴ ÷ 3.844 × 10⁸) = √(1.037 × 10⁶) = 1,018 m/s, or 1.02 km/s. The distance must be in metres, because GM is in m³/s².

afterFigure.text: Putting Earth’s radius into the formula gives 7.9 km/s just above the surface. The figure shows launches from the surface on either side of that speed: one at 4 km/s lands, one at 7.9 km/s circles the planet, and one at 10 km/s swings out to a long orbit that returns to the launch point.

lead.text: The International Space Station orbits about 400 km above the surface, and the distance that the formula needs is measured from Earth’s centre.

reveal.text: At 7.67 km/s the station covers 2π × 6,771 km = 42,544 km in 5,545 s, which is about 92 minutes for one orbit.

lead.text: The formula works for any central body, so Earth’s own motion round the Sun can be found from the Sun’s GM.

reveal.text: Circular speed falls as the square root of the distance, so Jupiter, at 5.2 AU, moves at 29.8 ÷ √5.2 = 13.1 km/s.

lead.text: An orbit returns to its start, and a spacecraft that is to leave a planet for good must climb out of its gravitational field entirely. The work needed to lift a mass m from distance r to an infinite distance is GMm ÷ r, a result that follows from adding up the force over the whole climb, and a mass launched with speed v has kinetic energy ½mv². Setting the two equal, the m cancels and **v = √(2GM ÷ r)**, the **escape speed**.

The escape speed is exactly *√2 times* the [[circular speed|The speed of a circular orbit, v = √(GM ÷ r). Met earlier in this lesson.]] at the same distance, about 1.414 times as large, because the 2 sits under the root. A body launched below it is bound to the planet and follows a closed orbit or falls back, while one launched at or above it leaves and never returns, slowing all the way.

afterFigure.text: From Earth’s distance from the Sun, escaping the Sun’s gravity requires 29.8 × √2 = 42.1 km/s. The figure compares a launch from Earth’s surface at the circular speed with one above the escape speed.

lead.text: The Moon’s pull on Earth is not the same everywhere. The side of Earth facing the Moon is nearer to it than Earth’s centre is, so it is pulled a little *harder* than the centre, and the far side is pulled a little *less* hard than the centre. Seen from the centre, the near water is drawn towards the Moon and the far water is left behind, so the oceans are stretched along the line to the Moon, into a bulge on each side of Earth.

These differences are small, about a ten-millionth of the pull of Earth’s own gravity, but the oceans can flow, and Earth turns beneath the two bulges once a day, so each coast meets two high tides and two low tides in about 25 hours. The pull itself follows the [[inverse-square law|A force that falls to a quarter when the distance doubles. Met in “Newton’s gravitation”.]], falling as 1/d², but **the difference between the pulls on the near and far sides falls faster, as 1/d³**, so a tide is much more sensitive to distance than the pull is.

cases.label: The Moon at its present distance
The Moon at about twice the distance

lead.text: The Sun raises tides in the same way, and the tide that a body raises is proportional to its mass divided by the cube of its distance. The Sun is about 2.7 × 10⁷ times as massive as the Moon but 389 times as far away, and 2.7 × 10⁷ ÷ 389³ = 0.46, so the Sun’s tide is **0.46 of the Moon’s**, which is large enough to matter.

At new moon and full moon the Sun and Moon lie on the same line through Earth, their stretches add, and the tides are at their largest, a **spring tide**, whose name has *nothing to do with the season*. At the quarters the Sun lies at right angles to the Moon, and its stretch partly cancels the Moon’s, giving the smallest range, a **neap tide**. In this idealised picture the two are in the ratio (1 + 0.46) ÷ (1 − 0.46) = 2.7.

cases.label: Moon today, Sun at right angles

lessons.orientation: Circular and escape speeds from the gravitational field, and tides as a difference in the Moon’s pull.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Gravity at the height of the International Space Station is still 89% as strong as at Earth’s surface, yet the astronauts aboard float, because the station and everything in it are *falling freely* towards Earth and never arrive. The station moves sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it as quickly as it falls, and that is what being in orbit means.

**How fast the sideways motion has to be** depends only on the pull of the planet and the distance from its centre, and the same field gives a second speed, the one at which a spacecraft leaves a planet altogether. A third result of the same law seems unrelated to either: the Moon pulls on the near side of Earth a little harder than on the far side, and that difference stretches the oceans into tides.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to find the speed of a circular orbit and the speed needed to escape, and explain tides.

recap.keyIdea: A circular orbit has speed √(GM ÷ r), escape needs √2 times as much, and a tide is the difference in the Moon’s pull across Earth, which varies as 1/d³.

blocks.text: In orbit a body is falling freely and missing the ground, which fixes the circular speed at v = √(GM ÷ r) in metres per second when r is in metres, and escape from the same distance needs v = √(2GM ÷ r), which is √2 times as much.

The Moon pulls the near side of Earth harder than the far side, and since that difference falls as 1/d³, the Moon’s tide exceeds the Sun’s, with the two adding to give [[spring tides|The largest tides, at new moon and full moon, when the Sun and Moon pull along the same line. Met in “Orbits, escape and tides”.]] and partly cancelling to give neap tides.

recap.nextHook: Gravity also weakens the light of a star as it spreads out, and the next lesson applies the same inverse-square rule to the brightness of a star and uses it, together with parallax, to measure how far away the stars are.

lessons.title: Brightness and distance

lead.text: Light from a small source spreads outwards in every direction, so the same total amount of light has to cover a larger and larger area as it travels. At a distance d the light has spread over **a sphere of radius d**, whose area is 4πd², and so the light falling on each square metre becomes thinner in proportion to 1 ÷ d².

Doubling the distance makes the sphere four times as large in area, so each square metre receives a *quarter* as much light. That is the same pattern as the [[inverse-square law|A quantity that falls to a quarter when the distance doubles. Met in “Newton’s gravitation”.]] of gravity, which also arises from an influence spreading over the surface of a sphere. The Sun’s light at 2 AU is therefore a quarter as intense as at 1 AU, as the figure shows.

Two quantities separate what a star gives out from *what reaches us*. The **luminosity** L of a star is the total power it radiates in all directions, measured in watts, and for the Sun it is 3.828 × 10²⁶ W, a value often used as a unit, the solar luminosity L☉. The **flux** F is the power that arrives on each square metre facing the star, measured in W/m².

At distance d the star’s power is spread over a sphere of area 4πd², so **F = L ÷ (4πd²)**. At 5 AU, which is 7.48 × 10¹¹ m and a little less than Jupiter’s distance, the area is 4π × (7.48 × 10¹¹)² = 7.03 × 10²⁴ m², and the flux from the Sun is 3.828 × 10²⁶ ÷ 7.03 × 10²⁴ = 54 W/m².

afterFigure.text: A telescope can measure a flux, while the distance d and the luminosity L are the quantities that we want, and the figure shows one luminosity at three distances. The next screens find d first, and L then follows.

reveal.text: That is the solar flux at the top of Earth’s atmosphere, 1,361 W/m², and by the inverse-square law Mars, at 1.52 AU, receives 1,361 ÷ 1.52² = 589 W/m².

lead.text: To use F = L ÷ (4πd²) we need d, and for the nearest stars it can be measured directly by geometry. As Earth goes round its orbit, a nearby star is seen from two points 2 [[AU|The average distance from Earth to the Sun, about 149.6 million km. Met in “Kepler’s laws”.]] apart, six months apart, and against the far more distant stars it appears to shift. Half of the shift is the star’s **parallax** p, the angle at the star between the Sun and Earth.

The angle is *tiny*, so it is measured in **arcseconds**, each one 1/3600 of a degree, and for so small an angle the triangle gives p = 1 AU ÷ d in radians. One arcsecond is 1/206,265 of a radian, so a star with a parallax of exactly one arcsecond is 206,265 AU away, a distance called a **parsec**, and in general **d = 1 ÷ p**, with d in parsecs and p in arcseconds. A parsec is 3.26 light-years, where a light-year is the distance that light travels in a year, 9.46 × 10¹² km.

afterFigure.text: In 1838 Friedrich Bessel measured the parallax of the star 61 Cygni and found about 0.31 arcsecond, which gives d = 1 ÷ 0.31 = 3.2 pc, or about 10.5 light-years, not far from the modern value of 11.4. Before then no parallax had been seen, and the failure to see one had long been used as an argument against a moving Earth.

lead.text: Proxima Centauri, the nearest star beyond the Sun, shifts against the background by a parallax that is measured to a thousandth of an arcsecond.

Rearranging F = L ÷ (4πd²) gives L = 4πd² × F, so a star whose distance and [[flux|The power that arrives on each square metre facing a star, F = L ÷ (4πd²). Met earlier in this lesson.]] have both been measured has a luminosity that can be computed. More often two stars are compared. Flux is proportional to L ÷ d², so a star that is 16 times as luminous as another but 4 times as far away has 16 ÷ 4² = 1 times the flux, and the two look equally bright.

Brightness in the sky is therefore *ambiguous*. A faint star may be a feeble one close by or a brilliant one far away, and **only the distance tells the two apart**. That is why parallax matters beyond the nearest stars, since it gives the first reliable distances, against which the methods for greater distances are checked.

reveal.text: Distance changes flux through its square, so a hundredfold difference in luminosity can be hidden by a tenfold difference in distance.

lessons.orientation: How a star’s brightness falls with distance, how parallax measures that distance, and how the two give luminosity.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A torch held close to a wall lights a small bright circle, and held farther back it lights a larger and dimmer one, although the torch itself has not changed. Every star behaves in the same way, so that its apparent brightness mixes two things, *how much light it gives out* and how far away it is, and a faint star may be either a feeble lamp near by or a brilliant one far off.

To separate the two, astronomers need **a measure of distance that does not depend on brightness**, and the most direct one is geometric. Brightness falls with distance by the same inverse-square rule as gravity, and a small shift in a star’s position gives the distances of the nearer stars; the two together reveal how much light a star really emits.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to find a star’s distance from its parallax and compare stars by luminosity and flux.

recap.keyIdea: Flux falls as the inverse square of the distance, F = L ÷ (4πd²), and a parallax of p arcseconds puts a star at 1 ÷ p parsecs, which turns a measured flux into a luminosity.

blocks.text: Light spreads over a sphere, so flux is the luminosity divided by 4πd², and a star’s apparent brightness mixes how much light it emits with how far away it is.

Parallax separates the two for the nearer stars: a shift of p arcseconds puts the star at 1 ÷ p [[parsecs|The unit of distance equal to 3.26 light-years, at which a star shows a parallax of one arcsecond. Met in “Brightness and distance”.]], and that distance turns a measured flux into a luminosity, L = 4πd²F.

recap.nextHook: Brightness is only one thing that a star’s light carries, and the next lesson reads its colour, which gives the temperature of the star, and the small shifts in its spectral lines, which give its motion.

lessons.title: Temperature, colour and motion

lead.text: Light is a wave, and its colour is set by its **wavelength**, the distance from one crest to the next, which for visible light runs from about 400 nm for violet to about 700 nm for red, where one **nanometre** is a billionth of a metre. A hot, dense body such as a poker or a star gives out light across a whole range of wavelengths, and the shape of that range depends on nothing but its temperature. A body that behaves in this way is called a **blackbody**.

A blackbody spectrum rises to a maximum and falls away on either side, and the wavelength at the maximum is the **peak wavelength**. The hotter the body, the *shorter* its peak wavelength, which is why the poker moves from red towards white as it heats and why the colour of a star tells us how hot it is.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows three stars. The coolest peaks in the infrared, beyond the red end of the visible range, the middle one peaks in the yellow, and the hottest peaks in the ultraviolet, beyond the violet.

lead.text: The relation between the two was found by Wilhelm Wien in 1893, and it is **λmax = b ÷ T**, where b = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K is a constant and the temperature T is in **kelvin**. The kelvin is the same size as a degree Celsius but starts from absolute zero, so that 0 °C is 273 K, and physical formulae use this scale. Because T is in the denominator, a hotter body has a *smaller* [[peak wavelength|The wavelength at which a glowing body’s spectrum is strongest. Met earlier in this lesson.]], as the last screen showed.

For example, at T = 9,000 K the peak is 2.898 × 10⁻³ ÷ 9,000 = 3.22 × 10⁻⁷ m, and multiplying by 10⁹ converts metres to [[nanometres|Units of a billionth of a metre, used for the wavelength of light. Met earlier in this lesson.]], giving 322 nm, in the ultraviolet. The same law applies to everyday bodies: a person at about 310 K peaks at 9,350 nm in the infrared, which is why thermal cameras can detect warm bodies in the dark.

reveal.text: The Sun’s peak lies in the blue-green part of the visible range, and the Sun looks white because it also gives out a great deal of light at the other visible wavelengths.

lead.text: Wien’s law can also be run backwards, from a measured peak to a temperature.

reveal.text: At 10,000 K the star peaks in the ultraviolet, and the visible light that it does give out looks blue-white.

lead.text: Starlight carries more than a colour. When it is spread into a spectrum, narrow dark or bright **spectral lines** appear at particular [[wavelengths|The distance from one wave crest to the next; it sets the colour of light. Met earlier in this lesson.]], because each kind of atom absorbs and emits light only at wavelengths that belong to it. Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen showed in 1859 that each chemical element makes its own pattern of lines, so a pattern in a star identifies the elements in it, and the line of hydrogen at 656.28 nm is one of the most familiar.

The pattern is fixed in the laboratory but not in the sky. When a star moves away from us its light waves are *stretched*, and every line shifts to a longer wavelength, which is called a **redshift**. When a star moves towards us the waves are squeezed, and the lines shift to a shorter wavelength, a **blueshift**. Christian Doppler proposed the effect in 1842.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows the hydrogen line for a star at rest, one receding at 1,000 km/s and one approaching at 1,000 km/s. The shift, about 2 nm in each direction, is small but measurable, and **it grows in proportion to the speed**.

lead.text: For a speed v far below the speed of light c, the fractional change in the wavelength of a [[spectral line|A narrow dark or bright line in a spectrum, at a wavelength fixed by one kind of atom. Met earlier in this lesson.]] equals the speed as a fraction of c, so Δλ ÷ λ = v ÷ c, where Δλ is the observed wavelength minus the laboratory wavelength and λ is the laboratory wavelength. Rearranged, **v = c × Δλ ÷ λ**, with c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s, and the result is the star’s **radial velocity**, its speed along the line of sight, which is positive when the star is receding and negative when it is approaching.

Take a stretch of 0.5%, which is a fraction of 0.005. The speed is 0.005 × 3.00 × 10⁵ = 1,500 km/s, and it is a receding one because the wavelength has grown. The method gives *only* the part of the motion along the line of sight, because movement across the sky does not change wavelengths.

reveal.text: A speed of 3,000 km/s is 1% of the speed of light, far too large for a star in our own Galaxy, where speeds are mostly tens of km/s, and it is typical of a distant galaxy, which the last two lessons return to.
The shift is only 0.25 nm in 500, or 0.05%, and detecting changes as small as this needs a spectrograph that separates wavelengths very finely.

lessons.orientation: How a star’s colour gives its surface temperature through Wien’s law, and how the shift of its spectral lines gives its speed.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A poker left in a fire glows a dull red, then orange, and if it could be heated far enough it would turn yellow-white and then blue-white. Its colour acts as a thermometer, since **the hotter the metal, the bluer its light**, and the same is true of a star, so that the colour of a star’s light gives the temperature of its surface without any instrument touching it.

Starlight carries a second kind of information. Dark and bright lines in a star’s spectrum sit at positions fixed by the atoms that make them, and when the star moves towards or away from us the whole pattern shifts a little, by an amount that gives the *speed* of the star along the line of sight. One formula gives the temperature from the colour, and another gives the motion from the shift.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to find a star’s temperature from its colour and its speed from the shift of a spectral line.

recap.keyIdea: A star’s peak wavelength is 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K divided by its temperature, and the fraction by which a spectral line is shifted equals the star’s radial speed as a fraction of the speed of light.

blocks.text: The hotter a star, the shorter the wavelength at which it peaks, by [[Wien’s law|The peak wavelength is 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K divided by the temperature in kelvin. Met in “Temperature, colour and motion”.]], so a star’s colour gives the temperature of its surface.

A spectral line shifts to a longer wavelength when the star recedes and to a shorter one when it approaches, and **v = c × Δλ ÷ λ** gives the radial velocity from the shift, positive for recession and negative for approach.

recap.nextHook: A star’s luminosity and its temperature are now both measurable, and the next lesson plots one against the other, which sorts the stars into groups and shows what their position says about their size.

lessons.title: The H–R diagram

lead.text: A star is a glowing ball, and the light it gives out leaves through its surface. Each square metre of a surface at temperature T radiates a power of σT⁴, where σ = 5.670 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant, a law that Josef Stefan found from experiment in 1879 and Ludwig Boltzmann derived in 1884. A sphere of radius R has a surface area of 4πR², so the [[luminosity|The total power a star radiates, in watts or in solar luminosities. Met in “Brightness and distance”.]] is **L = 4πR² × σT⁴**.

The Sun gives a check. At T = 5,772 K each square metre radiates 5.670 × 10⁻⁸ × 5,772⁴ = 6.29 × 10⁷ W, and its radius of 6.957 × 10⁸ m gives an area of 4π × (6.957 × 10⁸)² = 6.08 × 10¹⁸ m², so its luminosity is 6.29 × 10⁷ × 6.08 × 10¹⁸ = 3.83 × 10²⁶ W, which agrees with the 3.828 × 10²⁶ W found from its flux. The radius enters as a *square* because it fixes the area.

Comparing stars is easier in solar units, in which the Sun has a radius of 1 R☉, a temperature of 1 T☉ = 5,772 K and a luminosity of 1 L☉, and the law becomes **L = R² × (T ÷ T☉)⁴**, with L in L☉ and R in R☉. The radius enters as a square, because it fixes the area, and the temperature as a *fourth* power, because it fixes the power per square metre.

The fourth power makes **temperature far more influential**. A star ten times as wide has only 10² = 100 times the area, while a surface ten times hotter radiates 10⁴ = 10,000 times as much from each square metre. Both can act together: a star with twice the Sun’s radius and 1.5 times its temperature has L = 2² × 1.5⁴ = 4 × 5.06 = 20.25 L☉.
In solar units the law is L = R² × (T ÷ T☉)⁴.

Place each star on a chart with its surface temperature along the bottom and its [[luminosity|The total power a star radiates. Met in “Brightness and distance”.]] up the side. By long convention the temperature axis runs backwards, with the hottest stars on the left, and both axes are stretched so that each step multiplies the value by the same factor, since luminosities range from about a ten-thousandth to a million times the Sun’s. Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell, working independently in the 1910s, made the first such plots, and the chart is called the **H–R diagram** in their honour.

The stars do *not* scatter over the chart. Most of them, including the Sun, lie along a diagonal band that runs from hot and luminous at the upper left to cool and dim at the lower right, and this band is the **main sequence**.

afterFigure.text: The figure places three stars on the chart: the Sun, Sirius A, which is hotter and about 25 times as luminous, and Proxima Centauri, a cool star with about a six-hundredth of the Sun’s luminosity. All three lie on the main sequence.

lead.text: Because L = R² × (T ÷ T☉)⁴, a star’s temperature and luminosity together fix its radius. A star above the [[main sequence|The diagonal band of the H–R diagram where most stars lie. Met earlier in this lesson.]] is much more luminous than a main-sequence star of the same temperature, so its surface must be *far* larger, and the cool and luminous ones are called **giants**, or supergiants at the top. A star below the main sequence is far fainter than one of the same temperature on it, so it must be tiny, and the hot and faint ones are **white dwarfs**.

A typical white dwarf has a radius of about 0.01 R☉, which is about the size of Earth, yet it holds about as much mass as the Sun. The figure shows a giant with 25 times the Sun’s radius, the Sun itself, and a white dwarf with about a hundredth of it.

afterFigure.text: Both groups are stars in later stages of their lives, which the next lesson explains: the main sequence is where a star spends most of its life, and the giants and white dwarfs are what it becomes afterwards.

reveal.text: The huge R² outweighs the small T⁴ factor of 0.15 that comes from the cool surface, and the star shines with nearly ninety thousand times the Sun’s luminosity.
The result is about a fortieth of the Sun’s luminosity, so a white dwarf is hot but dim.
Each square metre of both stars radiates the same power, so the giant, with 25 ÷ 0.75 = 33 times the radius, has about 33² = 1,100 times the surface area and so about 1,100 times the luminosity.

lessons.orientation: How luminosity depends on radius and temperature, and what a star’s place on the H–R diagram says about its size.
