blocks.text: The last two lessons gave two numbers for a star: its surface temperature, read from its colour, and its luminosity, found from its flux and its distance. Plotting those two numbers against each other, one point for each star, produced one of the most useful pictures in astronomy, because the stars do *not* scatter over the page. Most of them fall along a single band, and the rest gather in separate groups above and below it.

A star’s position on such a chart says more than its temperature and its luminosity, because the two together say something about its **size**. The relation between luminosity, radius and temperature is what makes that possible: a hot star that is faint must be small, and a cool star that is bright must be enormous, so the groups above and below the band are stars of very different sizes.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to find a star’s luminosity from its radius and temperature, and read its size from the H–R diagram.

recap.keyIdea: A star’s luminosity in solar units is R² × (T ÷ T☉)⁴, so its temperature and luminosity fix its radius, and the H–R diagram sorts stars into the main sequence, giants and white dwarfs.

blocks.text: A star radiates σT⁴ from each square metre of a surface of area 4πR², and in solar units this becomes L = R² × (T ÷ T☉)⁴, in which the fourth power of the temperature outweighs the square of the radius.

Plotted with temperature against luminosity, the stars fall on the [[main sequence|The diagonal band of the H–R diagram where most stars lie, the Sun among them. Met in “The H–R diagram”.]], with **giants above it, which must be large, and white dwarfs below it, which must be small**.

recap.nextHook: Where a star lies on the diagram depends on its mass and its age, and the next lesson shows how the mass of a star sets its luminosity, its lifetime and the way it ends.

lessons.title: How mass sets a star’s life

lead.text: A main-sequence star shines because **fusion** in its core joins hydrogen nuclei into helium, and 0.7% of the mass of the hydrogen fused is released as energy, in accordance with E = mc². The Sun’s luminosity of 3.828 × 10²⁶ W therefore requires 3.828 × 10²⁶ ÷ (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 4.3 × 10⁹ kg of mass to be converted each second, which means fusing about 6 × 10¹¹ kg of hydrogen every second.

The fuel is the hydrogen in the core, about a tenth of the Sun’s mass, or 2 × 10²⁹ kg, and the star lasts for its fuel divided by its *burn rate*: 2 × 10²⁹ ÷ 6 × 10¹¹ = 3 × 10¹⁷ s, which is about **10 billion years**. This is the Sun’s **main-sequence lifetime**, and the question for other stars is how their fuel and their burn rate change with mass.

The fuel in a star grows in proportion to its mass M, but the rate at which it is burnt grows much faster, because a heavier star squeezes its core harder, and a hotter, denser core fuses far more quickly. Observations of main-sequence stars show that luminosity rises roughly as **L ∝ M³·⁵**, with L and M in solar units, a rule of thumb that is good to within a factor of two or three.

A star of 3 M☉ is therefore 3³·⁵ = 27 × 1.73 = 47 times as luminous as the Sun, and a star of half a solar mass is 0.5³·⁵ = 0.125 × 0.71 = 0.09 times as luminous. *Tripling* the mass gives nearly fifty times the light.

afterFigure.text: Along the main sequence of the [[H–R diagram|A chart of luminosity against temperature, on which most stars lie along the main sequence. Met in “The H–R diagram”.]], mass increases from the cool, dim lower right to the hot, luminous upper left, and the figure shows three stars placed along it, of about 0.12, 1 and 2 solar masses.

lead.text: A power of 3.5 is a cube multiplied by a square root.

The [[lifetime|The time a star spends fusing hydrogen in its core. Met earlier in this lesson.]] of a star is its fuel divided by its burn rate. The fuel is proportional to M and the burn rate, which is the luminosity, to M³·⁵, so the lifetime is proportional to M ÷ M³·⁵ = M⁻²·⁵. Taking the Sun’s lifetime as 10 billion years, the rule is **t ≈ 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵**, with M in solar masses. The exponent is negative because *a heavier star burns its fuel faster than its fuel grows*.
A star of 2 M☉ has M⁻²·⁵ = 1 ÷ 2²·⁵ = 1 ÷ 5.66 = 0.177, so it lasts 1.77 billion years, less than a fifth of the Sun’s life, although it holds twice the fuel.

afterFigure.text: The rule is a simplification, because the exponent changes a little with mass and the share of the star that can be burnt varies, but it captures the main fact that the most massive stars live the fastest.

lead.text: The rule can be turned round. If a lifetime is known, the mass follows by inverting the power: from t ÷ 10 billion years = M⁻²·⁵ it follows that M = (10 billion years ÷ t)^(1 ÷ 2.5) = (10 billion years ÷ t)⁰·⁴. For a star that stays on the main sequence for 1 billion years the ratio is 10, and M = 10⁰·⁴ = 2.5 M☉.

The reversal is how astronomers date star clusters. All the stars of a cluster formed together, so the stars that are just leaving the [[main sequence|The diagonal band of the H–R diagram where stars fuse hydrogen in their cores. Met in “The H–R diagram”.]] have a lifetime equal to the cluster’s age, and **the mass of the heaviest star still on the main sequence fixes the age of the cluster**.

When the hydrogen in the core is used up, the core can no longer hold the star up against its own weight. A star below about 10 M☉, such as the Sun, swells into a red giant, then sheds its outer layers into space and leaves its core as a [[white dwarf|A hot, faint star about the size of Earth that no longer fuses anything. Met in “The H–R diagram”.]], which slowly cools. The Sun will follow this path in about 5 billion years.

A star above about 10 M☉ goes on to fuse heavier elements until its core is iron, which cannot release energy by fusion, and then the core collapses in a **supernova**, an explosion that can briefly rival the light of a whole galaxy. If the core that remains is small enough, it is a **neutron star**, a ball more massive than the Sun but only about 20 km across. Above about 40 M☉ *nothing* halts the collapse, and the remnant is a **black hole**, a region from which not even light can escape.

afterFigure.text: These boundaries are approximate, because the end of a star’s life also depends on its composition, its rotation and any companion star. The figure shows the three outcomes, for stars of 3, 25 and 50 solar masses.

reveal.text: A star of 15 M☉ lasts only 10 billion years × 15⁻²·⁵ = 0.0115 billion years, about 11 million years, before this happens.

lessons.orientation: How a star’s mass sets its luminosity, its main-sequence lifetime, and the remnant it leaves.

blocks.text: The Sun has been on the main sequence for about 4.6 billion years and has fuel for roughly as long again, which makes it a middle-aged star. Other stars live on a very different scale: the most massive burn through their fuel in a few million years, while the least massive will still be shining when the universe is hundreds of times its present age. All of them are made of the same hydrogen, so something about their *masses* must set their lifetimes.

The surprise is that **the stars with the most fuel die first**. A star of ten solar masses starts with ten times the Sun’s hydrogen but shines a few thousand times as brightly, so it spends its larger supply far sooner, and the same comparison, made with two rules of thumb, lets you estimate any star’s lifetime from its mass and say what it will leave behind.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to estimate a star’s lifetime from its mass and say how stars of different masses end.

recap.keyIdea: A star’s luminosity rises as M³·⁵ and its fuel only as M, so its main-sequence lifetime falls as M⁻²·⁵, and its mass also decides whether it ends as a white dwarf, a neutron star or a black hole.

blocks.text: A star burns its hydrogen at a rate set by its luminosity, which grows roughly as M³·⁵, while its fuel grows only as M, so t ≈ 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵: a star of 2 solar masses lasts about 1.8 billion years, and the heaviest stars last only millions.

When the fuel runs out, a star below about 10 solar masses sheds its outer layers and leaves a white dwarf, a star of about 10 to 40 solar masses collapses in a [[supernova|The explosion that ends the life of a massive star as its core collapses. Met in “How mass sets a star’s life”.]] and leaves a neutron star, and a still heavier star leaves a black hole.

recap.nextHook: Stars rarely live alone, and the next lesson moves outward to the galaxies in which billions of them are gathered, and to the way the motion of those galaxies shows that the universe is changing.

lessons.title: Galaxies and Hubble’s law

lead.text: A **galaxy** is a vast system of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity. Our own, the Milky Way, is a disc about 100,000 light-years across that holds a few hundred billion stars, and the Sun lies about 26,000 light-years from its centre. Stars within a galaxy are separated by [[light-years|The distance that light travels in a year, 9.46 × 10¹² km. Met in “Brightness and distance”.]], but galaxies are separated by millions of them, so astronomers measure galaxy distances in megaparsecs, where one **megaparsec** (Mpc) is a million [[parsecs|The unit of distance equal to 3.26 light-years, at which a star shows a parallax of one arcsecond. Met in “Brightness and distance”.]], or 3.26 million light-years.

Light takes time to cross such distances, and a distance in light-years is therefore also the time in years that the light has been travelling. The Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighbour of the Milky Way at 0.05 Mpc, or about 160,000 light-years, is seen as it was 160,000 years ago, and a galaxy in the Virgo cluster, at about 16 Mpc, as it was some 50 million years ago. *The farther a telescope looks, the further back in time it sees.*
The Andromeda galaxy is the large spiral galaxy nearest to the Milky Way.

The spectral shifts of the last lesson were first measured for galaxies by Vesto Slipher, from 1912, and he found that most of them were [[redshifted|Shifted to longer wavelengths, as the light of a receding source is. Met in “Temperature, colour and motion”.]], which is to say that they were receding. In 1929 Edwin Hubble combined such velocities with distances for 24 galaxies and found that the velocity rises *in proportion to* the distance, a relation that Georges Lemaître had already predicted from theory in 1927. It is called **Hubble’s law**, and it states that **v = H₀ × d**.

The quantity H₀ is the **Hubble constant**, about 70 km/s per Mpc, so each megaparsec of distance adds about 70 km/s to a galaxy’s recession speed. A galaxy at 30 Mpc recedes at 70 × 30 = 2,100 km/s, and since H₀ carries the units km/s per Mpc, the Mpc cancels and v comes out in km/s. Hubble’s own first value was about 500 km/s per Mpc, which was too large because the distances then in use were too small.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows galaxies at 50 and 250 Mpc, and the second, being five times as far, recedes five times as fast.

lead.text: It is natural to ask why the speed should be proportional to the distance, and a model shows it. Draw dots on a rubber sheet and stretch the sheet *evenly*, so that every length on it grows by the same fraction in the same time. Dots that are 5 cm and 15 cm from a chosen dot, stretched by 20%, end up 6 cm and 18 cm away, so the near dot has moved 1 cm and the far one 3 cm.

Each gap grows in proportion to its own length, so in a given time the far dot has moved away three times as much as the near one, and **speed is proportional to distance**. That is exactly [[Hubble’s law|The recession speed of a galaxy is the Hubble constant times its distance, v = H₀d. Met earlier in this lesson.]], and it suggests that galaxies are not flying through space like fragments from an explosion but are being carried apart as the space between them stretches.

Every distant galaxy recedes from us, which might suggest that we sit at the centre of the expansion, but the sheet shows otherwise. Stand on any dot of the stretching sheet and every other dot moves away from you, with the far ones moving fastest, so each dot sees the same pattern as every other. Two dots that are 15 cm apart move apart by 3 cm under a 20% stretch, and they do so *whichever* of the two is taken as the observer.

The same holds for galaxies. An observer in a galaxy 100 Mpc away would also find the rest receding in proportion to their distances, with the Milky Way among them, so **no galaxy is at the centre**. The expansion is a stretching of the space between galaxies, and Hubble’s law holds from every position.

Hubble’s law works in either direction. A galaxy’s redshift gives its [[radial velocity|A star’s or galaxy’s speed along the line of sight, v = c × Δλ ÷ λ, positive when it recedes. Met in “Temperature, colour and motion”.]] through v = c × Δλ ÷ λ, and its speed then gives its distance through **d = v ÷ H₀**. A spectral line at 400.0 nm in the laboratory that arrives at 404.0 nm, for example, gives v = 3.00 × 10⁵ × 4.0 ÷ 400.0 = 3,000 km/s and d = 3,000 ÷ 70 = 43 Mpc, a distance that no parallax could measure.

The distance is *only as accurate as H₀*. Measurements based on the light of the early universe give about 67 km/s per Mpc, whereas measurements that build a ladder of distances out from nearby stars give about 73, a disagreement of roughly 9% that is called the **Hubble tension** and has not yet been explained.

afterFigure.text: The figure shows what the disagreement means for a single galaxy at 100 Mpc, whose predicted speed is 6,700 km/s with one value and 7,300 km/s with the other.

lead.text: Hubble’s law can be turned round, so that a measured speed gives a distance.

reveal.text: That difference, 1,800 km/s, is about 9% of the galaxy’s speed, which is why the choice between 67 and 73 matters for every distance and age worked out from H₀.

lessons.orientation: The scale of galaxies and lookback time, and Hubble’s law linking a galaxy’s recession speed to its distance.

blocks.text: On a dark night, far from city lights, a faint smudge can be seen in the constellation Andromeda. It is a galaxy of about a trillion stars, and the light that reaches your eye left it before our species existed, so what you see is **a picture of the galaxy as it was** and not as it is.

Galaxies like this one fill the universe in their hundreds of billions, and their light carries a second message. When it is spread into a spectrum, almost every galaxy shows its lines shifted to longer wavelengths, and the farther the galaxy, the larger the shift. The simplest reading of that pattern is that the space between the galaxies is stretching, and once the rate of stretching is known, the shift in a galaxy’s light gives its distance even when it is far too remote for any other method.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to turn a galaxy’s distance into its recession speed, and a redshift into a distance.

recap.keyIdea: A galaxy recedes at a speed proportional to its distance, v = H₀d, which follows from space stretching evenly and has no centre, and it gives distances from redshifts as d = v ÷ H₀.

blocks.text: Galaxies lie millions of light-years apart, so their light shows them as they were long ago, and [[Hubble’s law|The recession speed of a galaxy is the Hubble constant times its distance, v = H₀d. Met in “Galaxies and Hubble’s law”.]] says that each megaparsec of distance adds about 70 km/s to the speed at which a galaxy recedes.

An even stretch of space produces exactly this pattern and looks the same from every galaxy, so we are not at a centre, and a measured redshift gives a distance through d = v ÷ H₀, accurate only as far as the value of H₀ is known.

recap.nextHook: If the galaxies are moving apart now, then running the motion backwards brings them together, and the last lesson uses H₀ to find when that happened and what the universe was like then.

lessons.title: The age and afterglow of the Big Bang

lead.text: If a car is now 60 km from your door and has been driving straight away from it at a steady 40 km/h, it left 60 ÷ 40 = 1.5 hours ago, because the time taken is the distance divided by the speed. The same reasoning applies to a galaxy, on the assumption that it has always moved at its present speed, and the time since it was at our position is then its distance divided by its speed.

For a galaxy at distance d, [[Hubble’s law|The recession speed of a galaxy is the Hubble constant times its distance, v = H₀d. Met in “Galaxies and Hubble’s law”.]] gives v = H₀d, so the time is d ÷ (H₀d) = **1 ÷ H₀**, and the distance cancels. *Every* galaxy, near or far, gives the same answer, which is why the expansion can be dated at all: all the galaxies were together at one moment, and that moment is a time 1 ÷ H₀ ago, the **expansion age** of the universe.

reveal.text: For the galaxies each has its own distance and its own speed, and Hubble’s law makes the time come out the same for all of them.

lead.text: The [[Hubble constant|The number H₀ in Hubble’s law, about 70 km/s per Mpc. Met in “Galaxies and Hubble’s law”.]] has units of km/s per Mpc, and to get a time *the distance unit has to be removed*. One Mpc is 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km, so H₀ = 60 km/s per Mpc means 60 km/s for every 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km, and the kilometres cancel in 1 ÷ H₀ = 3.086 × 10¹⁹ km ÷ 60 km/s = 5.14 × 10¹⁷ s. That is in seconds, and one billion years is 3.156 × 10¹⁶ s, so dividing gives 16.3 billion years.

Doing the conversion once for every value of H₀ gives a constant, since 3.086 × 10¹⁹ ÷ 3.156 × 10¹⁶ = 977.8, and so **1 ÷ H₀ = 977.8 billion years ÷ H₀**, with H₀ in km/s per Mpc. A larger H₀ means a faster expansion and a shorter time, and a smaller H₀ a longer one.

reveal.text: That is close to the accepted age of the universe, and the next screen compares the two.

lead.text: For H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc the expansion age 977.8 ÷ 70 is about 14 billion years, and the accepted age of the universe is 13.8 billion years, found mainly from the microwave glow described below. The two nearly agree, but they ought not to agree exactly, because 1 ÷ H₀ assumes that every galaxy has moved at its present speed throughout, and the expansion has not been steady.

Gravity slowed the expansion in the first several billion years, which makes the true age *shorter* than 1 ÷ H₀. In 1998 two teams of astronomers found from distant supernovae that the expansion has been speeding up for about the last six billion years, a change attributed to **dark energy**, the name given to whatever drives it, and that makes the true age *longer*. The two effects nearly cancel, so 1 ÷ H₀ happens to land close to 13.8 billion years.

afterFigure.text: The [[Hubble tension|The disagreement between the values of H₀, about 67 and about 73 km/s per Mpc, found by different methods. Met in “Galaxies and Hubble’s law”.]] between 67 and 73 km/s per Mpc matters here too, since 977.8 ÷ 67 = 14.6 billion years and 977.8 ÷ 73 = 13.4 billion years, a spread of more than a billion years.

lead.text: A smaller Hubble constant means a slower expansion.

reveal.text: A slower expansion needs longer to spread the galaxies out to their present distances, which is why the age rises as H₀ falls.

lead.text: Run the expansion back far enough and the universe was smaller and also hotter, since squeezing a gas heats it. When it was about 380,000 years old it was a glowing gas at about 3,000 K, so opaque that light could not travel far. As the expansion cooled the gas below that temperature, electrons and nuclei combined into atoms, the gas became transparent, and the light that had been trapped streamed away in every direction.

That light is still travelling, and it reaches us from *every* direction as the **cosmic microwave background**. Its wavelengths have been stretched as space expanded, so the glow that began at 3,000 K now has the spectrum of a [[blackbody|An ideal glowing body whose spectrum depends only on its temperature. Met in “Temperature, colour and motion”.]] at 2.725 K, whose peak, by [[Wien’s law|The peak wavelength is 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K divided by the temperature in kelvin. Met in “Temperature, colour and motion”.]], lies in the microwave region.

afterFigure.text: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found the glow by accident in 1965, as a steady hiss in a radio antenna at Bell Laboratories that no direction of the sky could remove, and the COBE satellite showed in 1990 that its spectrum is the closest to a perfect blackbody ever measured.

reveal.text: A peak of about a millimetre lies in the microwave region, between the infrared and the radio waves, which gives the glow its name.

lead.text: While the light has crossed the expanding universe, its wavelengths have been stretched in the same proportion as space, much as the dots on the rubber sheet moved apart. By [[Wien’s law|The peak wavelength is 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K divided by the temperature in kelvin. Met in “Temperature, colour and motion”.]] the peak wavelength is inversely proportional to the temperature, so a stretch of the wavelengths by any factor lowers the temperature of the glow by *that same factor*.

A glow at 300 K, about the temperature of a room, peaks near 10 µm in the infrared, and stretched 100 times its peak moves to about 1 mm and its temperature falls to 3 K, which is the case shown in the figure. **The factor by which the background has been stretched since its release is therefore the earlier temperature divided by the temperature now.**

cases.label: The same glow stretched 100 times, 3 K

reveal.text: A stretch by a factor of about a thousand takes light from the visible and infrared ranges into the microwave range.

lessons.orientation: How 1 ÷ H₀ estimates the age of the universe, and how the cosmic microwave background is the stretched afterglow of its hot early state.
lessons.reviewLabel: The age and afterglow of the Big Bang

blocks.text: Hubble’s law says that every galaxy recedes at a speed proportional to its distance. Play the expansion **backwards** and every galaxy moves back towards us, and because the farther galaxies move faster in exactly the proportion that they are farther, they all return at the same moment, whatever their distance. That moment is the beginning of the expansion, which is what the name Big Bang describes.

The moment can be dated from H₀ alone, since the time taken to cover a distance at a steady speed is the distance divided by the speed. The estimate turns into a number of years that comes close to the accepted age of the universe, and the evidence from the other end of time agrees: the faint microwave glow left from the moment when the universe first became transparent.

intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to estimate the age of the universe from H₀ and read the temperature and stretch of the microwave glow.

recap.keyIdea: Running the expansion backwards gives an age of 1 ÷ H₀, about 14 billion years for H₀ = 70 km/s per Mpc and close to the accepted 13.8 billion, and the microwave background is the stretched afterglow of the hot early universe.

blocks.text: Because every galaxy’s speed is proportional to its distance, all of them were together a time 1 ÷ H₀ ago, which is 977.8 billion years ÷ H₀ with H₀ in km/s per Mpc. The true age is 13.8 billion years, because gravity slowed the expansion early on and dark energy has sped it up since, and the two effects nearly cancel.

The universe was a glowing gas of about 3,000 K when it became transparent, and the light of that glow has been stretched by a factor of about 1,100, so that its blackbody spectrum now peaks near a millimetre at 2.725 K, as the [[cosmic microwave background|The faint microwave glow from all directions, left over from when the universe became transparent. Met in “The age and afterglow of the Big Bang”.]].

questions.prompt: Cairo is at latitude 30° N. Roughly how high above the northern horizon does the north celestial pole stand there?
hints: At the equator the pole sits on the horizon, and at the North Pole it is overhead. Think about how far along that range Cairo’s latitude lies.

acceptedIdeas: About 30°
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 30°

choices.label: About 30°
About 60°
About 90°

questions.onCorrect: The pole stands about 30° above the horizon, the same as the latitude, and the next screen shows that this holds at every latitude.

misconceptions.feedback: 60° is 90° minus the latitude, which is the angle from the pole up to the zenith. The height asked for is measured up from the horizon.
90° is the pole’s height at the North Pole, where the latitude is 90°. Cairo lies much nearer to the equator.

questions.prompt: The sky turns about 15° an hour. Through what angle, in degrees, does a star move around its daily circle in 6 hours?
hints: The rate is constant through the night.
Multiply the rate by the time.
Calculate 15 × 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 15° per hour × 6 h = 90°, a quarter of a full circle.

questions.onCorrect: 90°. Steady turning means angle = rate × time, so 6 hours is a quarter of a circle.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the hours to the rate. They are different quantities: multiply them instead.
That divides the rate by the hours. The angle grows with time, so the hours multiply.

questions.prompt: From latitude 52° N, a star is circumpolar when its declination exceeds 90° − φ. What is that smallest declination, in degrees?
hints: The lowest point of the star's circle must stay above the horizon.
The lowest point lies 90° − δ below a pole that is φ high.
Subtract the latitude from 90°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: δ > 90° − 52° = 38°. Stars north of +38° never set from 52° N.

questions.onCorrect: 38°. The limit is measured from the pole, so subtract the latitude from 90°.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the latitude itself. The limit is measured from the pole, so the latitude has to be taken from 90°.
Only a star exactly at the pole would qualify under that limit. Every star close to it must qualify as well.

questions.prompt: A star of declination +20° crosses the meridian as seen from latitude 52° N. What is its altitude then, in degrees?
hints: The highest altitude comes on the meridian.
Find the difference between latitude and declination, then subtract it from 90°.
questions.onCorrect: 58°. Altitude on the meridian is 90° minus the gap between latitude and declination.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between latitude and declination. The altitude is what is left of 90° after the gap.
That adds latitude and declination. The rule uses the difference between them.

questions.prompt: Seen from latitude 30° N, a star of declination −10° crosses the meridian. Find its altitude in degrees.
hints: A southern declination enters with a minus sign.
The difference φ − δ is 30 − (−10).
Subtract that difference from 90°.
questions.onCorrect: 50°. A southern declination keeps its minus sign, so the gap is 40° and the altitude is 90° minus it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between latitude and declination. Take it away from 90°.
That treats −10° as +10°. A southern declination keeps its sign, which makes the gap larger.

questions.prompt: What single word names a star that never sets as seen from a given latitude?
hints: The star's circle stays around the pole without dipping below the horizon.

acceptedIdeas: circumpolar
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Circumpolar: its whole daily circle stays above the horizon around the celestial pole.

questions.onCorrect: Circumpolar: the whole daily circle stays above the horizon.

misconceptions.feedback: The meridian is a line across the sky, not a kind of star. The word you want describes a star that never sets.

questions.prompt: London lies at 51.5° N. Taking Earth’s tilt as 23.4°, find the Sun’s noon altitude at the June solstice, in degrees, to one decimal place.
hints: At the June solstice the Sun’s declination equals the tilt, north of the equator.
Find 51.5 − 23.4 first, then subtract it from 90.
questions.onCorrect: The gap between latitude and declination is 51.5° − 23.4° = 28.1°, and the noon altitude is 90° − 28.1° = 61.9°.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between latitude and declination. The altitude is measured up from the horizon, so the gap has to be taken away from 90°.
That is the noon altitude in December. In June the Sun’s declination is positive, which brings the Sun nearer to the zenith over London.

questions.prompt: Find the Sun’s noon altitude in London (51.5° N) at the December solstice, with a tilt of 23.4°, to one decimal place.
hints: In December the Sun’s declination is south of the equator, so it is negative.
Subtract that sum from 90°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At the December solstice δ = −23.4°. Altitude = 90° − |51.5° + 23.4°| = 90° − 74.9° = 15.1°.

questions.onCorrect: In December δ = −23.4°, so the gap is 51.5° + 23.4° = 74.9° and the noon altitude is 90° − 74.9° = 15.1°.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the noon altitude in June. In December the declination is negative, so the gap to London’s latitude is larger and the Sun stands lower.
That is the gap between latitude and declination, which still has to be taken away from 90° to give an altitude.

questions.prompt: At an equinox the Sun’s declination is 0°. Find the noon altitude of the Sun from latitude 40° N, in degrees.
hints: Set δ to zero.
The rule reduces to 90° − φ.
Subtract the latitude from 90°.
questions.onCorrect: At an equinox δ = 0°, so the rule reduces to 90° − φ = 90° − 40° = 50°.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the latitude. The altitude is measured up from the horizon, so the latitude has to be taken away from 90°.

questions.prompt: Imagine Earth had no axial tilt. What would the Sun’s noon altitude be in London (51.5° N) on every date, in degrees, to one decimal place?
hints: Without tilt the Sun never leaves the celestial equator.
Its declination is zero on every date.
Subtract the latitude from 90°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With no tilt δ = 0° all year, so the noon altitude is always 90° − 51.5° = 38.5°.

questions.onCorrect: With no tilt δ stays at 0° on every date, so the noon Sun always stands at 90° − 51.5° = 38.5°.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the latitude. Taking it away from 90° gives the altitude of a Sun that stays on the celestial equator.
That is London’s noon altitude in June, which exists only because of the tilt. With no tilt the Sun never leaves the celestial equator.

questions.prompt: At what northern latitude, in degrees, is the noon Sun directly overhead at the June solstice, taking Earth’s tilt as 23.4°? Give one decimal place.
hints: Directly overhead means an altitude of 90°.
Set 90° − |φ − δ| equal to 90°.
The latitude must match the Sun’s declination on that date.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Overhead means altitude 90°, so |φ − δ| = 0 and φ = δ = 23.4° N, the Tropic of Cancer.

questions.onCorrect: The Sun is overhead where latitude equals declination, which at the June solstice is 23.4° N, the Tropic of Cancer.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the Sun’s altitude when it is overhead, and the question asks for a latitude.
The equator has the Sun overhead at the equinoxes. At the June solstice the declination is positive, so the overhead point has moved north.

questions.prompt: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January. Why is it winter in the northern hemisphere then?
hints: Compare the two hemispheres: they have opposite seasons at the same distance from the Sun.

acceptedIdeas: The northern hemisphere tilts away from the Sun, so sunlight arrives low and days are short
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Seasons follow the tilt. In January the north leans away from the Sun: a low noon Sun spreads its energy thinly over short days, while the 3% change in distance matters little.

choices.label: The Sun gives out less energy in January
The northern hemisphere tilts away from the Sun, so sunlight arrives low and days are short
Earth's orbit carries it farthest from the Sun in January

questions.onCorrect: Seasons follow the tilt. In January the north leans away from the Sun, so noon sunlight is low and the days are short.

misconceptions.feedback: The Sun’s output hardly changes through the year, and the two hemispheres would not have opposite seasons if it did.
The question says that Earth is closest to the Sun in January, so distance cannot be what makes the north cold then.

questions.prompt: When the Sun–Earth–Moon angle is 90°, what percentage of the Moon’s visible disc is lit?
hints: At new moon, θ = 0°, none of the visible disc is lit, and at full moon, θ = 180°, all of it is.
An angle of 90° is halfway between the two.
Picture the Moon a week after new moon, when it stands a quarter of the way round its orbit, and look at how much of the face you see is lit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Lit fraction = (1 − cos 90°)/2 = (1 − 0)/2, half the disc.

questions.onCorrect: At 90° the Moon is a quarter of the way round its cycle and half of the visible disc is lit, which the formula on the next screen confirms: (1 − cos 90°) ÷ 2 = 0.5.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be the whole disc, which is lit only when θ = 180°. A quarter of the way round the cycle is not yet there.
25% is the share lit at θ = 60°. At 90° the Moon is halfway from new to full, so more of the lit half is turned towards us.

questions.prompt: The synodic month is 29.53 days. How many degrees per day does the Moon gain on the Sun? Give one decimal place.
hints: In one synodic month the Moon gains one full turn on the Sun.
A full turn is 360°.
Divide 360 by the number of days.
questions.onCorrect: One full turn of 360° shared over 29.53 days gives 360° ÷ 29.53 = 12.19°, which rounds to 12.2° a day.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole turn. The question asks how much of it the Moon gains in a single day.
That is the number of days. The rate is the full turn divided by that number of days.

questions.prompt: At which phase of the Moon can a lunar eclipse happen? Answer with one word.
hints: Earth’s shadow points directly away from the Sun.

acceptedIdeas: full
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Full: Earth must sit between the Sun and the Moon so the Moon can pass through Earth's shadow.

questions.onCorrect: At full moon Earth lies between the Sun and the Moon, so the Moon can pass through Earth’s shadow.

misconceptions.feedback: At new moon the Moon is between Earth and the Sun, while Earth’s shadow points away from the Sun and lies on the far side of Earth.

questions.prompt: The Moon is 3,475 km across and 384,400 km away. Find its angular diameter in degrees, to two decimal places, using angle ≈ diameter/distance and 1 radian = 57.3°.
hints: Divide the diameter by the distance to get radians.
Convert radians to degrees with the factor 57.3.
Round the result to two decimal places.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the angle in radians. Multiplying it by 57.3 converts it to degrees.

questions.prompt: How many days after new moon is first quarter, taking the synodic month as 29.53 days? Give two decimal places.
hints: First quarter is a Sun–Earth–Moon angle of 90°.
That is one quarter of the full cycle.
Divide the synodic month by 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: First quarter is a quarter of the cycle: 29.53 ÷ 4 = 7.3825, about 7.38 days.

questions.onCorrect: First quarter is a quarter of the way round the cycle, and 29.53 ÷ 4 = 7.3825, which rounds to 7.38 days.

misconceptions.feedback: That is half of the cycle, the full moon. First quarter comes sooner.
That is three quarters of the cycle, the third quarter. First quarter comes sooner.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the Moon’s visible disc is lit when the Sun–Earth–Moon angle is 120°?
hints: Use (1 − cos θ)/2.
The cosine of 120° is −0.5.
Convert the fraction to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: At 120° the cosine is −0.5, so (1 + 0.5) ÷ 2 = 0.75 and 75% of the disc is lit.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats cos 120° as +0.5. The cosine of an angle above 90° is negative, which makes more of the disc lit.
That would be the share at 90°. At 120° more of the lit half has turned towards us.

questions.prompt: An asteroid’s orbit has semi-major axis 2 AU and eccentricity 0.6. How close does it come to the Sun, in AU?
hints: The Sun sits at a focus, a × e from the centre.
Perihelion distance is a(1 − e).
Calculate 2 × (1 − 0.6).

misconceptions.feedback: That is a × e, the distance from the centre of the ellipse to the Sun. The closest point is that far short of a.
That is the far end of the orbit. The closest point lies on the near side of the Sun.

questions.prompt: For the orbit with a = 2 AU and e = 0.6, the speed at perihelion divided by the speed at aphelion equals the aphelion distance divided by the perihelion distance. Find this ratio.
hints: Aphelion is a(1 + e) and perihelion is a(1 − e).
Work out both distances.
Divide 3.2 by 0.8.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Aphelion 3.2 AU ÷ perihelion 0.8 AU = 4. The asteroid moves four times faster at its closest point.

questions.onCorrect: Aphelion 3.2 AU ÷ perihelion 0.8 AU = 4, so the asteroid moves four times as fast at its closest point.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio upside down. The planet moves faster at the closer end, so the ratio must be greater than 1.
That is the aphelion distance in AU, and the question asks for a ratio of the two distances.

questions.prompt: An asteroid orbits the Sun with semi-major axis 4 AU. Using P² = a³ (P in years, a in AU), find its period in years.
hints: Cube the semi-major axis.
That gives P².
Take the square root of 64.
questions.onCorrect: P² = 4³ = 64, so P = √64 = 8 years.

misconceptions.feedback: That is P², and the question asks for P itself, so take the square root.
That is the square root of a. The law cubes a first and then takes a square root.

questions.prompt: A planet orbits a star of 4 solar masses with a = 1 AU. Using P² = a³/M, find its period in years.
hints: Divide a³ by the star’s mass in solar masses.
1 cubed is 1.
Take the square root of a quarter.
questions.onCorrect: P² = 1³ ÷ 4 = 0.25, so P = 0.5 years, half of Earth’s year.

misconceptions.feedback: That is P², and the period is its square root.
That is the period around a Sun-like star. A heavier star divides P² by its mass, which shortens the period.

questions.prompt: Jupiter’s orbital period is 11.86 years. Using P² = a³, find its semi-major axis in AU, to two decimal places.
hints: Square the period to get a³.
11.86² is about 140.7.
Take the cube root of that.
questions.onCorrect: a³ = 11.86² = 140.7, so a is the cube root of 140.7, which is 5.20 AU.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a³. The semi-major axis is its cube root.
That is the square root of the period. Since P² = a³, a is the cube root of P², and not the square root of P.

questions.prompt: What name is given to the point of a planet’s orbit closest to the Sun?
hints: It begins with the Greek prefix for 'near'.

acceptedIdeas: perihelion
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Perihelion, from Greek peri (near) and helios (Sun). The farthest point is aphelion.

questions.onCorrect: Perihelion comes from the Greek peri, near, and helios, the Sun, and the farthest point is aphelion.

misconceptions.feedback: Aphelion is the farthest point. The closest point has the prefix that means near.

questions.prompt: Two bodies are moved from separation r to 3r. What happens to the gravitational force between them?
hints: Look again at the opener: the Moon is about 60 times as far from Earth’s centre as the apple, and it falls about 3,600 times less far in a second.
Ask what has to be done to 60 to give 3,600, and do the same to 3.

acceptedIdeas: It falls to a ninth of its value
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls to a ninth of its value

choices.label: It falls to a third of its value
It falls to a ninth of its value
It grows three times larger

questions.onCorrect: Tripling the separation divides the force by 3² = 9, because the pull weakens with the square of the distance, as the next screen shows.

misconceptions.feedback: A third would mean the force falls in proportion to the distance, whereas it falls with the square of the distance, so tripling the separation divides it by 9.
Moving the bodies apart weakens the pull between them, so the force falls rather than grows.

questions.prompt: At a fixed separation, one mass is doubled and the other tripled. By what factor does the gravitational force change?
hints: The force is proportional to the product of the masses.
Each mass change multiplies the force.
Multiply the two factors.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: F ∝ Mm, so the force changes by 2 × 3 = 6.

questions.onCorrect: Force is proportional to the product of the masses, so the factors multiply: 2 × 3 = 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the factors. The force depends on the product of the two masses, so the factors multiply.

questions.prompt: Earth’s GM is 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² and its radius is 6,371 km. Find g = GM/R² at the surface, in m/s², to two decimal places.
hints: Convert the radius to metres first.
Square 6.371 × 10⁶ m.
Divide GM by that square.

misconceptions.feedback: The radius must be in metres to match GM. In kilometres the radius is a thousand times too small, and g comes out a million times too large.

questions.prompt: Earth is about 81 times as massive as the Moon. How does Earth’s pull on the Moon compare with the Moon’s pull on Earth?
hints: Think of the pair as a tug of war between two bodies.
Whatever force acts on one body from the other, the other feels a force from it.
Newton’s third law pairs the two forces.

acceptedIdeas: The two pulls are equal in size
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The two pulls are equal in size

choices.label: Earth’s pull is about 9 times as large
The two pulls are equal in size
Earth’s pull is about 81 times as large

questions.onCorrect: The two forces are an equal and opposite pair, since GMm ÷ r² is the same whichever body is called M.

misconceptions.feedback: The factor of 81 belongs to the masses, and it shows up in how much each body accelerates, not in the size of the pull, since GMm ÷ r² is the same whichever body is called M.
The force depends on the product of the two masses, which is the same number whichever body you start from, so the two pulls are equal.

questions.prompt: Mars has GM = 4.283 × 10¹³ m³/s² and radius 3,390 km. Find its surface gravity in m/s², to two decimal places.
hints: Use g = GM/R² with R in metres.
Square 3.39 × 10⁶.
Divide GM by that square.

misconceptions.feedback: The radius must be in metres to match GM. In kilometres the answer comes out a million times too large.

questions.prompt: Why do a hammer and a feather dropped together on the Moon land together?
hints: Divide the gravitational force by the falling object’s own mass.

acceptedIdeas: The pull on each is proportional to its mass, so the acceleration GM/r² is the same for both
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Force GMm/r² divided by the object's mass m leaves GM/r², the same for any object at that place. With no air there is no drag to separate them.

choices.label: Heavier objects are pulled less strongly per kilogram
The pull on each is proportional to its mass, so the acceleration GM/r² is the same for both
The Moon's gravity does not act on light objects

questions.onCorrect: Dividing the pull GMm ÷ r² by the object’s mass m leaves GM ÷ r², which is the same for any object.

misconceptions.feedback: Gravity acts on light and heavy objects alike, and the Moon pulls on the feather in proportion to its mass, just as it pulls on the hammer.
Dividing GMm ÷ r² by m removes the object’s own mass, so no object is pulled more weakly per kilogram than another.

questions.prompt: Find the circular orbital speed 400 km above Earth, where r = 6,771 km and GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², in km/s, to two decimal places.
hints: Use v = √(GM/r) with r in metres.
Divide GM by 6.771 × 10⁶ m.
Take the square root and convert from m/s to km/s.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in metres per second. Divide by 1,000 to give km/s.

questions.prompt: Find the escape speed from Earth’s surface, with R = 6,371 km and GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², in km/s, to two decimal places.
hints: Use v = √(2GM/r).
Double GM, then divide by the radius in metres.
Take the square root and convert to km/s.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the circular speed at the surface, and escaping needs more than staying in orbit.
That is in metres per second. Divide by 1,000 for km/s.

questions.prompt: Using v = √(GM/r) with GM☉ = 1.327 × 10²⁰ m³/s² and r = 1.496 × 10¹¹ m, find Earth’s orbital speed in km/s, to one decimal place.
hints: This is a circular-orbit speed around the Sun.
Divide GM☉ by the distance in metres.
Take the square root, then divide by 1,000.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in metres per second. Divide by 1,000 to give km/s.

questions.prompt: Tidal stretching falls as the cube of distance. If the Moon were at half its present distance, by what factor would its tides grow?
hints: A tide is a difference in pull across Earth.
That difference scales as one over distance cubed.
Cube the factor of 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Tide ∝ 1/d³, so halving d multiplies the tide by 2³ = 8.

questions.onCorrect: A tide is a difference in pull, which scales as 1/d³, so half the distance gives 2³ = 8.

misconceptions.feedback: That squares the factor, as for the pull itself, but a tide is a difference in pull, which falls faster with distance.
That follows 1/d. The difference in pull falls faster than that, as 1/d³.

questions.prompt: The Moon has GM = 4.90 × 10¹² m³/s² and radius 1,737 km. Find the escape speed from its surface in km/s, to two decimal places.
hints: Escape speed is √(2GM/R).
Convert the radius to metres.
Compute the square root and convert to km/s.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the circular speed at the surface. The escape speed is larger.

questions.prompt: Why are the tides largest around new moon and full moon?
hints: Think about where the Sun lies relative to the Earth–Moon line at those phases.

acceptedIdeas: The Sun's and the Moon's tidal stretches line up and add
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At new and full moon the Sun, Earth and Moon are in line, so the solar tide (0.46 of the lunar tide) adds to the Moon's: spring tides. At the quarters they partly cancel: neap tides.

choices.label: The Sun's and the Moon's tidal stretches line up and add
Earth spins faster at those phases
The Moon is always closest to Earth at those phases

questions.onCorrect: At new and full moon the Sun, Earth and Moon are in line, so the Sun’s tidal stretch adds to the Moon’s.

misconceptions.feedback: The Moon’s distance varies over the month, but not in step with its phase. Look at where the Sun lies at new and full moon.
Earth’s spin does not change with the Moon’s phase. Look at where the Sun lies relative to the Moon.

questions.prompt: A probe moves from 1 AU to 2 AU from the Sun. What fraction of the solar flux it received at 1 AU does it now receive?
hints: Light spreads over a sphere of area 4πd².
Doubling d multiplies that area by 2².
Take the reciprocal of 2².

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Flux ∝ 1/d², so it falls to 1/2² = 1/4 = 0.25 of its value at 1 AU.

questions.onCorrect: 0.25. Flux follows 1/d², so doubling the distance divides the flux by four.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves the flux. It follows the inverse square, so the 2 is squared.
That makes the flux grow. It weakens as the star gets farther.

questions.prompt: The Sun’s luminosity is 3.828 × 10²⁶ W. Find the flux at 1 AU = 1.496 × 10¹¹ m, in W/m², to the nearest whole number.
hints: Use F = L/(4πd²).
Square the distance in metres, then multiply by 4π.
Divide the luminosity by that area.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the 4π. The light has spread over a whole sphere, whose area is 4πd².

questions.prompt: Proxima Centauri’s parallax is 0.768 arcseconds. Find its distance in parsecs, to two decimal places.
hints: Distance in parsecs is the reciprocal of parallax in arcseconds.
Divide 1 by the parallax.
Round to two decimal places.
questions.onCorrect: d = 1 ÷ 0.768 = 1.302 pc, about 1.30 pc, which is 4.25 light-years.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the parallax itself. The distance is its reciprocal.

questions.prompt: Star A is 100 times as luminous as star B, yet they appear equally bright. How many times farther away than B is A?
hints: Flux is proportional to L/d².
Keep the flux fixed while L grows a hundredfold.
Then d² must grow by the same factor; take the square root.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Equal flux needs L/d² equal, so d grows as √L: √100 = 10 times farther.

questions.onCorrect: Equal flux needs L ÷ d² equal, so d grows as √L, and √100 = 10 times as far.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the luminosity factor. Flux falls as 1/d², so the distance factor is smaller.
That squares the factor. The distance must grow as the square root of the luminosity factor, not its square.

questions.prompt: A star’s parallax is 0.05 arcseconds. Find its distance in light-years, to one decimal place, using 1 pc = 3.26 ly.
hints: First convert parallax to parsecs with d = 1/p.
Then multiply by 3.26 light-years per parsec.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance in parsecs. Convert it to light-years with 1 pc = 3.26 ly.
That multiplies the parallax by 3.26. The distance in parsecs is the reciprocal of the parallax.

questions.prompt: What unit of distance is defined as the distance at which a star shows a parallax of one arcsecond?
hints: Its name joins the first syllables of the two words that define it.

acceptedIdeas: parsec
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The parsec: PARallax of one arcSECond. It equals 206,265 AU or 3.26 light-years.

questions.onCorrect: The parsec takes its name from a parallax of one arcsecond, and it equals 206,265 AU, or 3.26 light-years.

misconceptions.feedback: A light-year is also a distance, but it is defined by how far light travels in a year, and not by a parallax.

questions.prompt: Using Wien’s law λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K / T, find the peak wavelength of the Sun (T = 5,772 K) in nanometres, to the nearest whole number.
hints: Divide Wien’s constant by the temperature.
The result comes out in metres.
Multiply by 10⁹ to convert metres to nanometres.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in metres. Multiplying by 10⁹ turns metres into nanometres.

questions.prompt: A star’s spectrum peaks at 290 nm. Find its surface temperature in kelvin, to the nearest hundred.
hints: Rearrange Wien’s law for T.
Write the peak wavelength in metres.
Divide the constant by that wavelength, then round.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 2.90 × 10⁻⁷ = 9,993 K, which is 10,000 K to the nearest hundred.

questions.onCorrect: T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ ÷ 2.90 × 10⁻⁷ = 9,993 K, which is 10,000 K to the nearest hundred.

misconceptions.feedback: Round your answer to the nearest hundred, as the question asks.

questions.prompt: A hydrogen line with laboratory wavelength 656.28 nm is observed at 662.84 nm. Using v = cΔλ/λ with c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s, find the radial velocity in km/s, to the nearest ten (positive means receding).
hints: Find the shift: observed minus laboratory wavelength.
Divide the shift by the laboratory wavelength.
Multiply by the speed of light in km/s.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Δλ = 6.56 nm; v = 3.00 × 10⁵ × 6.56/656.28 = 2,999 km/s, which is 3,000 km/s to the nearest ten, receding.

questions.onCorrect: Δλ = 6.56 nm, and v = 3.00 × 10⁵ × 6.56 ÷ 656.28 = 2,999 km/s, which is 3,000 km/s to the nearest ten.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the shift in nanometres. Divide it by the laboratory wavelength, then multiply by c.
The line moved to a longer wavelength, which is a redshift, so the star is receding and the velocity is positive.

questions.prompt: A star approaches at 150 km/s. Find the shift of its 500.00 nm line in nanometres, with redshift positive and blueshift negative, to three decimal places. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s.
hints: An approaching source has a negative radial velocity.
Use Δλ = λv/c.
Multiply 500 by −150, then divide by 300,000.
questions.onCorrect: Δλ = 500 × (−150) ÷ 300,000 = −0.250 nm, which is a blueshift.

misconceptions.feedback: The star is approaching, so the line moves to a shorter wavelength and the shift is negative.

questions.prompt: Betelgeuse looks orange-red and Rigel looks blue-white. What does the difference tell you?
hints: Which property of a glowing body sets where its spectrum peaks?

acceptedIdeas: Betelgeuse's surface is cooler, so its spectrum peaks at longer wavelengths
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Colour tracks surface temperature through Wien's law: about 3,600 K for Betelgeuse against about 12,000 K for Rigel. Their radial speeds are far too small to change a colour.

choices.label: Betelgeuse is farther away, so its light has reddened on the way

questions.prompt: A star twice the Sun’s radius has a luminosity of 4 L☉. Taking T☉ = 5,772 K, find its surface temperature in kelvin.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4 = 2² × (T/T☉)⁴ gives (T/T☉)⁴ = 1, so T equals the Sun's temperature: 5,772 K.

questions.onCorrect: 4 = 2² × (T ÷ T☉)⁴ gives (T ÷ T☉)⁴ = 1, so T equals the Sun’s temperature, 5,772 K.

misconceptions.feedback: That scales the temperature with the radius. Luminosity depends on R² and on T⁴ separately.

questions.prompt: A star has the Sun's radius and the Sun's temperature. What is its luminosity in solar units?
hints: Put R = 1 and T = T☉ into the formula.

acceptedIdeas: One solar luminosity
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One solar luminosity

choices.label: One solar luminosity
Zero
Four solar luminosities

questions.onCorrect: With R = 1 and T = T☉ both factors are 1, so L = 1 L☉: the Sun itself.

misconceptions.feedback: Both factors are 1 here. Nothing multiplies the result by four.
The Sun shines, and a star identical to it must do the same.

questions.prompt: Why does temperature count for more than radius?
hints: Compare the exponents in L = R²(T/T☉)⁴.

acceptedIdeas: T is raised to the fourth power and R only to the second.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: T is raised to the fourth power and R only to the second.

choices.label: Hot stars are bigger.
The Sun's temperature is the largest.
T is raised to the fourth power and R only to the second.

questions.onCorrect: A fourth power grows faster than a square, so a change in T moves L more than the same change in R.

misconceptions.feedback: Hot stars are not necessarily bigger. The reason is in the exponents.
Many stars are hotter than the Sun. The reason is in the exponents.

questions.prompt: Where on the H–R diagram are the hottest stars?
hints: Temperature runs backwards on this diagram.

acceptedIdeas: On the left
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: On the left

choices.label: At the bottom
On the left
On the right

questions.onCorrect: The temperature axis runs backwards, so the hottest stars are on the left.

misconceptions.feedback: Cool stars are on the right, because the temperature axis runs backwards.
Height shows luminosity, not temperature. Look along the horizontal axis.

questions.prompt: A star has half the Sun’s radius and twice the Sun’s surface temperature. Find its luminosity in solar units.
hints: Use L = R²(T/T☉)⁴ with R = 0.5 and T/T☉ = 2.
Work out each factor separately.
Multiply the radius factor by the temperature factor.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the radius factor alone. The hotter surface multiplies it.
That is the temperature factor alone. The smaller radius divides it.

questions.prompt: A comet comes within 1 AU of the Sun at its closest and moves out to 9 AU at its farthest. How long is the long axis of its orbit, in AU?
hints: Picture the long line through the two ends, with the Sun on it.
The comet’s closest and farthest points are the two ends.
Add the two distances.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two ends are 1 AU and 9 AU from the Sun, on either side of it: 1 + 9 = 10 AU.

questions.onCorrect: The nearest and farthest points lie at opposite ends of the long axis, with the Sun between them, so 1 + 9 = 10 AU.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the difference of the two distances. The Sun lies between the two ends of the axis, so the distances add.
That is only the far end. The long axis also includes the stretch from the Sun to the nearest point.

questions.prompt: What is the eccentricity of a perfect circle?
hints: Eccentricity measures how stretched the ellipse is.

acceptedIdeas: Zero
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Zero

choices.label: One
Zero
One half

questions.onCorrect: A circle is not stretched at all, so e is zero.

misconceptions.feedback: An eccentricity near 1 means a long, thin ellipse, the opposite of a circle.
A half-way value is a fairly stretched ellipse, not a circle.

questions.prompt: Why does aphelion use (1 + e)?
hints: Where is the Sun, compared with the centre of the ellipse?

acceptedIdeas: The Sun is off-centre by a × e, so the far end is a + a × e from it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Sun is off-centre by a × e, so the far end is a + a × e from it.

choices.label: The Sun is off-centre by a × e, so the far end is a + a × e from it.
Because aphelion is measured from the planet.
Because e is always larger than 1.

questions.onCorrect: The Sun is a × e from the centre, so the far end is that much farther than a.

misconceptions.feedback: e is between 0 and 1 for an ellipse. The 1 + e comes from the Sun's off-centre position.
Both distances are measured from the Sun. The planet is at the point being measured.

questions.prompt: Where does a planet move slowest?
hints: Where is the line from the Sun to the planet longest?

acceptedIdeas: At aphelion
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At aphelion

choices.label: At perihelion
It moves at the same speed everywhere
At aphelion

questions.onCorrect: A long line sweeps the same area with a short arc, so the planet is slowest at aphelion.

misconceptions.feedback: At perihelion the line is shortest, so the planet moves fastest.
Equal areas in equal times needs the speed to change as the distance does.

questions.prompt: A comet has perihelion 0.5 AU and aphelion 7.5 AU. Find its semi-major axis, in AU.
hints: The long axis runs from the near end to the far end through the Sun.
Add the two distances to get the long axis.
a is half the long axis.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The long axis is 0.5 + 7.5 = 8 AU, and a is half of it: 4 AU.

questions.onCorrect: The long axis is 0.5 + 7.5 = 8 AU, and a is half of it, 4 AU.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole long axis. The semi-major axis is half of it.
That is the difference of the two distances. The long axis is their sum.

questions.prompt: A full cycle from one new moon to the next takes about 30 days. How many days pass between a new moon and the next full moon?
hints: New moon to new moon is the whole cycle.
Full moon sits opposite the Sun, halfway round.
Halve the 30 days.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Full moon is halfway through the cycle: 30 ÷ 2 = 15 days.

questions.onCorrect: Full moon comes halfway through the cycle, when the Moon is opposite the Sun, so 30 ÷ 2 = 15 days after new moon.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole cycle, from one new moon to the next. Full moon comes part of the way through it.
That is a quarter of the cycle, the first quarter. Full moon comes later than that.

questions.prompt: Which angle θ between Sun and Moon gives a new moon?
hints: At new moon, none of the lit half faces us.
questions.onCorrect: At θ = 0° the Moon is in line with the Sun and we see only its dark side.

misconceptions.feedback: At 90° half the disc is lit: a quarter phase, not new.
At 180° the Moon is opposite the Sun and fully lit: full moon.

questions.prompt: Why is more than half the disc lit when θ = 150°?
hints: What happens to the lit half as θ grows past 90°?

acceptedIdeas: Beyond 90° we see more of the lit half than the dark half.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Beyond 90° we see more of the lit half than the dark half.

choices.label: Beyond 90° we see more of the lit half than the dark half.
The Moon is closer to Earth then.
The Sun shines more brightly then.

questions.onCorrect: Past 90°, the lit half is turned more towards us than away, so more than half the disc shows.

misconceptions.feedback: Distance does not set the phase. The angle does.
The Sun's brightness does not change. What changes is how much of the lit half we face.

questions.prompt: After one synodic month, what does the Moon show?
hints: The synodic month is the time from one new moon to the next.

acceptedIdeas: The same phase as before
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same phase as before

choices.label: A new phase every time
The opposite phase
The same phase as before

questions.onCorrect: After 29.53 days the Sun–Moon angle has gained a full turn, so the phase repeats.

misconceptions.feedback: The opposite phase comes halfway through the month, after half a turn.
The cycle repeats exactly. Each month brings the same sequence.

questions.prompt: The Moon is 3,475 km across. If it were twice as far as 384,400 km, what would its angular diameter be, in degrees, to two decimal places? Use 1 radian = 57.3°.
hints: Double 384,400 km first.
Divide the diameter by that new distance, then multiply by 57.3.
Round to two decimal places.
questions.onCorrect: Twice the distance halves the angular size: 3,475 ÷ 768,800 = 0.00452 radians, and × 57.3 is 0.259°, about 0.26°.

misconceptions.feedback: That would make the Moon look larger. A greater distance makes it look smaller.
That is the size at the real distance, and doubling the distance changes it.

questions.prompt: A planet has Earth’s mass but twice Earth’s radius. By what factor does its surface gravity change compared with Earth’s?
hints: Surface gravity is g = GM/r², and M is unchanged.
Doubling r changes g by the inverse square.
Square the 2, then take the reciprocal.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: g = GM/r², so doubling r divides g by 2² = 4, a factor of 0.25.

questions.onCorrect: g = GM ÷ r², so doubling r divides g by 2² = 4, a factor of 0.25.

misconceptions.feedback: That halves g, as if gravity fell in proportion to the distance, whereas it falls with the square of the distance.
That makes g larger. A larger radius puts the surface farther from the centre, where the field is weaker.

questions.prompt: Which change weakens the gravitational force between two masses?
hints: Look at where r sits in the formula.

acceptedIdeas: Moving them farther apart
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Moving them farther apart

choices.label: Moving them farther apart
Making G larger
Making one of them heavier

questions.onCorrect: Force grows with the masses and falls as r² grows, so more separation weakens it.

misconceptions.feedback: A heavier mass increases the product Mm, which strengthens the pull.
G is a fixed constant. We cannot change it.

questions.prompt: Why do we multiply the factors?
hints: In F = GMm/r², how are the quantities combined?

acceptedIdeas: Each change scales the force on its own, so the effects multiply.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each change scales the force on its own, so the effects multiply.

choices.label: Because the formula adds the masses.
Because force is the sum of two terms.
Each change scales the force on its own, so the effects multiply.

questions.onCorrect: The force is a product and a quotient, so separate changes multiply together.

misconceptions.feedback: The formula multiplies the masses, it does not add them.
F is built from a product and a quotient, not a sum.

questions.prompt: In g = GM/r², what does M stand for?
hints: Which mass cancelled when we divided by m?

acceptedIdeas: The mass of the body doing the pulling
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The mass of the body doing the pulling

choices.label: The mass of the Sun
The mass of the falling object
The mass of the body doing the pulling

questions.onCorrect: M belongs to the body whose gravity we are measuring, such as Earth. The falling mass has cancelled.

misconceptions.feedback: The falling mass is m, and it cancelled when we divided by it.
The Sun is just one possible pulling body. M is whichever body's gravity you are measuring.

questions.prompt: Two bodies are moved from separation r to 4r. By what factor does the gravitational force between them change? Give four decimal places.
hints: Gravity follows an inverse-square law.
Square the factor by which the distance grew.
Take the reciprocal of 4².
questions.onCorrect: Force follows 1/r², so four times the separation divides the force by 4² = 16, a factor of 0.0625.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 4, but the force follows the inverse square of the separation.
That makes the force grow. It weakens as the bodies move apart, so the factor is below one.

questions.prompt: Earth’s surface curves away by 5 m over every 8 km, and a ball falls 5 m in its first second. How fast, in km/s, must the ball travel along the ground to keep missing it?
hints: In one second the ball falls 5 m.
The ground must curve away by 5 m in that same second.
How far along the ground does it take for the surface to curve away by 5 m?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The ground curves away 5 m over 8 km, and the ball falls 5 m in 1 s, so it must cover 8 km each second: 8 km/s.

questions.onCorrect: The ball falls 5 m in 1 s while the ground curves away 5 m in 8 km, so it covers 8 km each second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the drop in metres. The speed is the distance travelled along the ground in one second.

questions.prompt: A satellite moves slower than the circular speed at its height. What happens?
hints: Gravity pulls it inward faster than its path curves away.

acceptedIdeas: It falls towards the body
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It falls towards the body

choices.label: It falls towards the body
It stays on a circle
It escapes

questions.onCorrect: Too slow and the pull wins: the path curves into the body instead of round it.

misconceptions.feedback: Escape needs more speed than the circular speed, not less.
A circle needs exactly the circular speed. Slower, the path bends inward.

questions.prompt: Why must r be in metres?
hints: Check the units of GM.

acceptedIdeas: GM is in m³/s², so r must be in metres too.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: GM is in m³/s², so r must be in metres too.

choices.label: GM is in m³/s², so r must be in metres too.
Metres are the biggest unit.
Square roots only work on metres.

questions.onCorrect: The formula works in SI units. GM is in m³/s², so r must be in metres for the answer to be in m/s.

misconceptions.feedback: Metres are not the biggest unit. The reason is the units of GM.
A square root works on any positive number. The units of GM are what matter.

questions.prompt: A probe moves at exactly the escape speed. What happens to it?
hints: The path opens out rather than closing.

acceptedIdeas: It never returns
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It never returns

choices.label: It circles at a fixed height
It falls back
It never returns

questions.onCorrect: At the escape speed the path just fails to close, so the probe never returns.

misconceptions.feedback: A circle needs the smaller circular speed.
Falling back needs a speed below the circular speed.

questions.prompt: A satellite circles Earth at r = 8,000 km from Earth’s centre. Find its speed in km/s, to two decimal places. GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s².
hints: Use v = √(GM/r) with r in metres.
Divide GM by 8 × 10⁶ m.
Take the square root and convert from m/s to km/s.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the escape speed at this distance. The circular speed is smaller.
That is in metres per second. Divide by 1,000 for km/s.

questions.prompt: The noon Sun’s overhead point moves from the Tropic of Cancer, 23.4° N, to the Tropic of Capricorn, 23.4° S. Through how many degrees of latitude does it travel?
hints: Where is the Sun overhead in June, and where in December?
The two tropics lie on opposite sides of the equator.
Add the two distances from the equator.
questions.onCorrect: The overhead point travels 23.4° + 23.4° = 46.8°, twice the tilt, because it crosses the equator between the two tropics.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance from the equator to one tropic. The journey from one tropic to the other crosses the equator and covers more than that.

questions.prompt: What is the Sun's declination around 21 December?
hints: In December the northern hemisphere leans away from the Sun.
questions.onCorrect: −23.4°. The Sun is south of the celestial equator by the tilt in December.

misconceptions.feedback: That is June. In December the northern hemisphere leans away, so the Sun is south of the equator.

questions.prompt: Why is the Sun's declination +23.4° in June?
hints: Think about which way the tilted axis points.

acceptedIdeas: The northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun.

choices.label: Earth is closest to the Sun then.
The Sun moves north through space.
The northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun.

questions.onCorrect: The axis keeps its direction while Earth orbits, so in June the north leans towards the Sun.

misconceptions.feedback: Distance does not set the declination. Earth is nearest the Sun in January.
The Sun is not moving. Earth's tilted axis makes it appear to shift north and south.

questions.prompt: Which noon Sun spreads the same beam of sunlight over more ground: London’s (51.5° N) at the June solstice, or the equator’s at an equinox?
hints: Find each Sun’s noon altitude first. At an equinox the Sun’s declination is 0°.
The lower of the two Suns spreads the beam more.

acceptedIdeas: The noon Sun in London at the June solstice
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The noon Sun in London at the June solstice

choices.label: The noon Sun at the equator at an equinox
The noon Sun in London at the June solstice
Both spread it equally

questions.onCorrect: London’s June Sun stands at 61.9°, while the equator’s equinox Sun is overhead at 90°, so London’s beam covers about 1.1 times its own width and the equator’s only its own width.

misconceptions.feedback: At an equinox the Sun’s declination is 0°, the same as the equator’s latitude, so the noon Sun there is directly overhead and spreads the beam over no more than its own width. London’s June Sun, at 61.9°, is lower.

questions.prompt: Sydney lies at 33.9° S, so φ = −33.9°. Find the noon Sun’s altitude there at the June solstice, in degrees, to one decimal place.
hints: Southern latitudes take a minus sign, and so does the subtraction that follows.
Work out −33.9 − 23.4 and ignore its sign.
Subtract that size from 90.
questions.onCorrect: With φ = −33.9° and δ = +23.4° the gap is 57.3°, so the noon altitude is 90° − 57.3° = 32.7°.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between latitude and declination, which still has to be taken away from 90° to give an altitude.
That is Sydney’s noon altitude in December. In June the Sun’s declination is positive, which puts it far from a southern latitude.

questions.prompt: Star X has 3 times the fuel of star Y and burns it 12 times as fast. How long does X’s fuel last compared with Y’s? Give a decimal.
hints: Lasting time is fuel divided by burn rate.
Take Y’s fuel and rate as 1, so X’s are 3 and 12.
Divide 3 by 12.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Lifetime = fuel ÷ burn rate = 3 ÷ 12 = 0.25 of Y's.

questions.onCorrect: Lifetime is fuel ÷ burn rate, so X lasts 3 ÷ 12 = 0.25 as long as Y.

misconceptions.feedback: That is upside down. More fuel lengthens the life, and a faster burn shortens it.
That multiplies the fuel by the rate. Fuel lengthens the time and burn rate shortens it, so the two are divided.

questions.prompt: A star has more mass than the Sun. How does its main-sequence life compare?
hints: Compare how fast fuel and burn rate grow with mass.

acceptedIdeas: Shorter
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Shorter

choices.label: The same
Shorter
Longer

questions.onCorrect: Burn rate grows much faster than fuel, so heavier stars live shorter lives.

misconceptions.feedback: More fuel, yes, but the burn rate grows far faster. The burn rate wins.
Burn rate depends strongly on mass, so lifetimes differ.

questions.prompt: Why is the exponent in M⁻²·⁵ negative?
hints: Divide M by M³·⁵.

acceptedIdeas: Fuel grows as M but burn rate as M³·⁵, so lifetime falls as M rises.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fuel grows as M but burn rate as M³·⁵, so lifetime falls as M rises.

choices.label: Mass is measured in solar units.
Fuel grows as M but burn rate as M³·⁵, so lifetime falls as M rises.
Lifetimes are always small numbers.

questions.onCorrect: M ÷ M³·⁵ = M⁻²·⁵: the burn rate outgrows the fuel, so the lifetime shrinks.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign has nothing to do with size. It comes from dividing M by M³·⁵.
Solar units set the scale, not the sign of the exponent.

questions.prompt: Using L ∝ M³·⁵, how many times the Sun’s luminosity does a 10 M☉ main-sequence star have? Give the nearest hundred.
hints: Raise the mass ratio to the power 3.5.
Split 10³·⁵ into 10³ × 10⁰·⁵.
Multiply 1,000 by √10, then round to the nearest hundred.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 10 by 3.5. The exponent is a power applied to 10.
That is 10³. The exponent is 3.5, which adds a square root of 10.

questions.prompt: If the sky makes one full turn of 360° in 24 hours, through how many degrees does it turn in one hour?
hints: The turning is steady, so every hour gets an equal share.
Share the 360° equally between the 24 hours.
Work out 360 ÷ 24.
questions.onCorrect: Shared equally over 24 hours, a full turn of 360° gives 360° ÷ 24 = 15° each hour, a rate used throughout the lesson.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole turn, which takes a day to complete. The question asks how much of it is covered in a single hour.
That is the number of hours in the turn, whereas the answer is an angle.

questions.prompt: A camera in Amsterdam is left pointing north with its shutter open for a few hours, and every star trail curves about one point in the sky. Which point is it?
hints: Think about what Earth’s axis points at.

acceptedIdeas: The north celestial pole
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The north celestial pole

choices.label: The brightest star in the northern sky
The zenith, straight above the camera
The north celestial pole

questions.onCorrect: Earth’s axis points at the north celestial pole, so every trail curves about it, and from Amsterdam the pole stands well below the zenith.

misconceptions.feedback: The point the trails curve about is a point in the sky and not a star. Polaris lies within a degree of it, which is why Polaris seems hardly to move, but it is not the point itself, and it is not the brightest star in the northern sky either.
