questions.prompt: Why can we multiply 15° by the number of hours?
hints: What would change if the sky sped up?

acceptedIdeas: The turning is steady, so every hour adds the same angle.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The turning is steady, so every hour adds the same angle.

choices.label: Stars move faster later in the night.
Multiplying always gives a bigger answer.
The turning is steady, so every hour adds the same angle.

questions.onCorrect: Steady turning means each hour adds the same angle, so the total is rate × hours.

misconceptions.feedback: A bigger answer is not the reason. Multiplying works because the rate does not change.
The sky turns at a constant rate. A changing rate would break the multiplication.

questions.prompt: A star has a declination of +90°. Where is it in the sky?
hints: Think about what +90° means for latitude on Earth.

acceptedIdeas: At the north celestial pole
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At the north celestial pole

choices.label: At the south celestial pole
On the celestial equator
At the north celestial pole

questions.onCorrect: A declination of +90° is the north celestial pole itself, the point that the whole sky turns about, so a star there would not circle.

misconceptions.feedback: The celestial equator lies at declination 0°. A declination of +90° is as far north as the sky extends.
The south celestial pole lies at −90°. The plus sign places a star on the northern side of the celestial equator.

questions.prompt: A star has turned through 270° of its daily circle. How many hours is that, at 15° per hour?
hints: How many 15° steps fit into the angle?
Divide, rather than multiply.
Work out 270 ÷ 15.
questions.onCorrect: 18 hours. Time is the angle shared out by the rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the angle by the rate. To find a time, share the angle out by the rate.
That adds the rate to the angle. Divide to find how many hours fit.

questions.prompt: A navigator measures Polaris 41° above the horizon. Taking Polaris to be at the north celestial pole, what is the ship’s latitude, in degrees north?
hints: Which angle did the last screen say equals the latitude?
The pole’s altitude equals the observer’s latitude.
The navigator measured the pole’s altitude directly.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pole’s altitude equals the latitude, so the ship is at the latitude the navigator measured.

questions.onCorrect: The ship is at latitude 41° N, because the pole’s altitude equals the latitude and a single measurement of Polaris therefore gives it directly.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 90° minus the altitude, the angle from Polaris up to the zenith. The latitude equals the altitude itself, with nothing subtracted.

questions.prompt: From latitude 40° N, what is the smallest declination, in degrees, that makes a star circumpolar?
hints: The star’s lowest point has to stay above the horizon.
The condition was δ > 90° − φ.
Put φ = 40° into the right-hand side.
questions.onCorrect: From 40° N the limit is 90° − 40° = 50°, so every star north of +50° stays above the horizon all night.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the latitude itself. The condition subtracts the latitude from 90°.
Adding the two angles gives a value above 90°, which no star can reach. The condition subtracts the latitude from 90° instead.

questions.prompt: At 15° an hour, how many hours does the sky take to turn through 135°?
hints: How many 15° steps fit into 135°?
Divide the angle by the rate.
Work out 135 ÷ 15.
questions.onCorrect: Each hour covers 15° of the turn, so 135° ÷ 15° per hour = 9 hours.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the angle by the rate. Each hour covers a fixed share of the turn, so the time needed is the angle divided by the rate.

questions.prompt: From latitude 30° N, what is the smallest declination, in degrees, that makes a star circumpolar?
hints: A star is circumpolar when its lowest point stays above the horizon.
The limit is a declination, measured from the celestial equator, that depends on the latitude.
Subtract the latitude from 90°.
questions.onCorrect: From 30° N the limit is 90° − 30° = 60°, so only stars north of +60° never set, fewer than at 40° N.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the latitude itself. The condition subtracts the latitude from 90°.
Adding the two angles gives a value above 90°, which no star reaches. The condition subtracts the latitude from 90° instead.

questions.prompt: On the equator the north celestial pole sits on the horizon. How many stars are circumpolar there?
hints: Where would the lowest point of any star’s circle fall, compared with the horizon?

acceptedIdeas: None
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: None

choices.label: None
About half of them
Only the stars very near the north celestial pole

questions.onCorrect: None. On the equator the limit is 90°, and no star has a declination above that, so every star rises and sets.

misconceptions.feedback: Half of the sky is above the horizon at any moment, but each star still spends part of every turn below it, so no star stays up all the time.
A star close to the pole traces a small circle, but on the equator that circle is centred on the horizon, so half of it still lies below.

flashcards.front: From latitude 41° N, how many degrees above the horizon is the north celestial pole?
flashcards.back: The pole's altitude equals the latitude: 41°.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pole's altitude equals the latitude: 41°.

courseChecks.title: Find your starting point
courseChecks.description: Twelve problems from the turning sky to the age of the universe. Find which ideas need attention before you begin.

question.prompt: From latitude 40° N, how many degrees above the horizon is the north celestial pole?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pole stands as high above the horizon as the latitude: 40°.

question.prompt: At latitude 30° N, with Earth's tilt taken as 23.4°, find the Sun's noon altitude at the June solstice, in degrees, to one decimal place.
What percentage of the Moon's visible disc is lit when the Sun–Earth–Moon angle is 45°? Give one decimal place.
A body orbits the Sun with semi-major axis 16 AU. Using P² = a³, find its period in years.
The distance between two bodies shrinks to a quarter of its first value. By what factor does the gravitational force between them change?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: F ∝ 1/r², so a quarter of the distance gives 4² = 16 times the force.

question.prompt: The drawing shows a 9 km/s launch from 1,000 km above Earth, which stretches into an ellipse. Find the circular orbital speed at that height, where r = 7,371 km and GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², in km/s, to two decimal places.

A star has five times the Sun's radius and the Sun's surface temperature. Find its luminosity in solar units.
Using t ≈ 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵, find the main-sequence lifetime of a 2 M☉ star in billions of years, to two decimal places.

courseChecks.title: Bring the ideas together
courseChecks.description: Twelve mixed problems across the sky, orbits, starlight and the cosmos. Record your confidence; results appear after the final response.

question.prompt: Using t ≈ 10 billion years × M⁻²·⁵, find the main-sequence lifetime of a 10 M☉ star in millions of years, to the nearest whole number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10²·⁵ = 316.2, so t = 10,000 million/316.2 = 31.6, about 32 million years.

question.prompt: The drawing shows a 3 km/s launch from the surface of Mars, which falls back. Mars has GM = 4.283 × 10¹³ m³/s² and radius 3,390 km. Find the escape speed from its surface in km/s, to two decimal places.
From latitude 60° N, what is the smallest declination, in degrees, of a star that never sets?
A source recedes at 1,500 km/s. Using λ = λ₀(1 + v/c) with c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s, at what wavelength is its 400.00 nm line observed, in nm, to two decimal places?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Δλ = 400.00 × 1,500/300,000 = 2.00 nm, so the line appears at 402.00 nm.

A comet comes within 1 AU of the Sun and reaches 5 AU at its farthest. Find its orbital period in years, to two decimal places, using P² = a³.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The long axis is 1 + 5 = 6 AU, so a = 3 AU and P = √27 = 5.196, about 5.20 years.
